activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Ireland's Great Famine began in 1845 when potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety, the Lumper, whose lack of genetic variety left it vulnerable.
story:
Mr. Perera had pushed the desks into a circle and taped a map of the vacant lot behind the school to the whiteboard, and now the seminar belonged, at least in theory, to whoever spoke first. That was Aiden, because he had spent two evenings drafting a proposal and could not bear to watch it wilt in his notebook while Salma and Iris and the others circled around it like water around a stone.

"Beans," he said, laying his notes flat on his knee. "The whole lot, or most of it. They fix nitrogen, they're cheap, everybody will eat them, and the food bank said they'd take as many as we can grow. One crop, one plan, no guesswork."

Salma leaned forward with her elbows on the desk. "One crop across an entire lot. You're sure about that."

"I'm sure it's reliable," Aiden said, and heard how thin it sounded, like he was describing a machine he had only read about.

Iris, who had said almost nothing all term, turned her chair a few degrees toward him. "My gran's from Mayo. She says the reason the Famine was so bad there wasn't only that the potatoes failed. Ireland's Famine began in 1845, when the blight struck a whole population that lived on one potato variety." She paused, picking at the sleeve of her jumper. "The Lumper, it was called. A lot of people, one potato. And the Lumpers were all so alike that when the blight came, there was nothing in them that could resist it."

The circle went quiet in the way rooms do when someone mentions a death at a dinner party. Aiden felt something shift under his argument, a floorboard loosening, though he couldn't yet have said what had been holding it up.

"That's not the same thing," he said, more slowly now. "We're not depending on this to survive. It's a garden."

"But you picked beans for the same reason they picked the Lumper," Iris said. "Because it was dependable. Because it fed the most people for the least trouble." She wasn't being scathing about it; her voice was almost gentle, which somehow made it worse, or better, he couldn't decide. "Dependable and fragile aren't opposites."

Mr. Perera, who had a habit of standing by the window with his arms folded as if the discussion were weather happening some distance away, wrote the word "monoculture" on the corner of the whiteboard and then, apparently thinking better of handing it to them as a gift, underlined nothing and stepped back.

Aiden looked down at his notes. Two evenings of work. Rows and yields and a letter to a hardware store about donated fencing. He had been so pleased with the logic of it, and he was beginning to see that the logic was not wrong exactly, only built for a question nobody in this room had asked yet. The real question, he thought, was what the garden was for. Food, obviously. But food for whom, at what risk, chosen by which arguments, and who paid if the choosing turned out badly? It was strange to feel a single potato variety reaching all the way into a seminar room a hundred and seventy-some years later, tugging at his bean rows.

"Okay," he said. "Here's what I still think. Splitting the lot five ways means less food this year, and the food bank doesn't care about our education, it cares about kilograms. That part of my plan stands." He turned his palm up. "But here's what I'm giving up. If we plant everything, we're betting the whole harvest on one set of genes and one kind of luck. So what if the middle is rows of beans, like before, and the borders are whatever anyone wants to bring from home. Seeds from someone's grandmother. Things nobody would choose for yield. A hedge, even."

"That's not a compromise," Salma said, "that's a portfolio."

"Is that cynical?" Aiden asked the circle, honestly wanting to know. "Picking diversity as a strategy. It's like, is it still a good thing if you do it for cold reasons?" He was thinking of a word his ethics teacher had used that he'd disliked at the time, some flavor of relativism, the idea that values were just tools you picked according to the job, and he had argued then that some things had to be held absolutely. He hadn't expected the garden to make him less sure.

Iris shrugged. "The blight didn't care why the Lumpers were all the same."

"Then it doesn't matter why we're mixed," Salma said.

"It matters to me," Aiden said, surprised at himself. "I want to want the mixed garden, not just need it. I don't know yet which one I'm doing."

Mr. Perera uncapped a marker and drew a border around the plot on the map, then left the middle blank. He handed the marker to Aiden without a word.

Aiden stood at the whiteboard for a moment, the cap warm in his palm. Then he drew three long rows through the empty center, and in the margins, slowly, without deciding, he began to write the things people might bring.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream's surface speed typically reaches about 2.5 metres per second at its fastest, making it one of the fastest ocean currents.
story:
The field trip sheet said Planetarium, Session Three: Ocean Circulation, and Parker had signed up because Mr. Banerjee had hinted that the unit test would draw on it. He stood with Aleksandar and Makenna in front of a wall-sized map of the North Atlantic, where the currents were drawn as ribbons of colour, red for warm water pushing north along the edge of the Americas, blue for cold water sinking back south of Greenland. On paper it looked simple. In his notes it looked like nothing.

"You're supposed to be able to explain how this warms Europe," Makenna said. She tapped the red ribbon that curved toward Norway. "There's a station where you talk into a microphone and it records you. Ten people get picked to have theirs played for the whole group."

Parker read the panel beside the map. It gave the surface speed of the Gulf Stream at its fastest, about 2.5 metres per second, which a smaller line translated into terms a visitor could feel in the legs: roughly a brisk walking pace. He stood in front of that line for a while. Aleksandar came over and read it too.

"So it moves as fast as I walk to the bus stop," Aleksandar said. "That's it? I thought it would be, like, a river in fast-forward."

"It's one of the fastest ocean currents," Parker said. "That's the point. That's the fastest it gets, and the whole ocean is doing that, all the time, in the dark, whether anyone's measuring it."

Makenna had already gone to the microphone station, a small booth with a green light, and her voice came back through the speakers mid-sentence, something about heat being carried like freight. Parker listened and found he didn't believe her, though he couldn't have said why. The map's arrows made the ocean look like plumbing, a system you could reify into pipes and valves, and that was exactly what was bothering him. Water wasn't a pipe. The warm ribbon touched cold water the whole way north, and touching meant mixing, and mixing meant the story couldn't just be about delivery.

He walked the map again, following the red ribbon from Florida past Newfoundland toward the Norwegian coast. Behind him a class of younger students was herded past a display on biomes, a wall of photographs, savanna grassland giving way to taiga, and a docent saying something about latitude and climate that Parker half heard. Latitude. He stopped. London sat at roughly the same latitude as the southern tip of the savanna photographs, far north of anywhere that should be green and temperate, yet London was famously mild and grey and cosmopolitan, a city of people from everywhere who had come, in some part, because the weather let them. Same latitude, different world. The difference was the red ribbon under his finger.

But that was the part he didn't trust, and he made himself say it plainly to Aleksandar at the microphone booth. "The current brings the heat. I get that part. What I don't get is whether that's the whole reason or just a piece of it, because the wind has to matter too, and the map doesn't show wind."

"So say that," Aleksandar said. "The booth doesn't grade you."

Parker stepped in when the light went green. He kept it short. The Gulf Stream moved north carrying warm surface water, and at its fastest its surface speed reached about 2.5 metres per second, about the speed of a person walking quickly, which made it one of the fastest ocean currents anywhere. That warm water gave up its heat to the air over the northeastern Atlantic, and the wind carried that air across toward Europe, so that places as far north as London and Norway stayed far warmer than the same latitudes on the other side of the ocean. Then he said the part he was least sure of and said it anyway: he did not know how to weigh the current against the winds, and he suspected neither did anyone who hadn't spent years on it.

He came out. Mr. Banerjee was standing by the biome wall with his clipboard, and he had clearly heard, because he said, "You hedged at the end." Parker said that he had, and that the hedge was true. Mr. Banerjee marked something and did not argue.

At the end of the session a docent chose six recordings to play to the whole group in the dome. Parker's was fifth. He sat between Aleksandar and Makenna and listened to his own voice fill the curved ceiling, the numbers and the walking pace and the confession of uncertainty, and when the lights came up Makenna leaned over and said, "Yours sounded like a person actually thinking." Outside, in the parking lot, he looked at the sky over the school and could not see any of it.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The ashes were in a shoebox between Seth's feet, because the proper container had been backordered, and his mother said the funeral home's insistence on ceremony was the kind of thing Grandma would have mocked for a week. They had been driving for two hours already, north toward the lake where she had wanted them scattered, and the dashboard said they had forty minutes left. Seth turned the box slightly so the lid faced up, then turned it back, unsure which way respect pointed.

He had not told his mother about Friday. On Friday, four days after the funeral, Mika and Ryder had dragged him to a late movie, and somewhere in the second act he had laughed, actually laughed, loud enough that a man two rows down shushed him. He had spent the rest of the film with his jaw clenched, and the walk home afterwards felt like something he should confess to. His grandmother had been dead nine days. Nine days, and he had laughed at a comedy about a disaffected weatherman who quits on live television.

The flashback came without warning, the way hers always did. He was eleven, riding in this same back seat, and Grandma was in the front arguing with the radio pundit about some election, calling him a pompous windbag, delighted with her own outrage. She had turned around and said, "Seth, when I die, don't you dare mope for a year. Mope for a decent interval, then go do something interesting and tell me about it at the grave, because I'll be bored otherwise." Eleven-year-old Seth had said that was creepy, and she had laughed her gravelly laugh and gone back to harassing the pundit, who could not hear her.

His mother was quiet in a way that was not peaceful. She kept adjusting the mirror, then the vent, then the mirror again, and when a talk station came on she snapped it off so fast the knob clicked. "She wanted this lake," his mother said, to the windshield. "You know she almost bought the property in eighty-nine. Your grandfather problematized it for a month, every flood risk and septic question, and by the time he was satisfied, someone else had it." Seth knew the story. He also knew, though he had never said so, that his mother had wanted to sell Grandma's house immediately, before the estate was even settled, and that she had not slept well since doing the paperwork anyway. She wanted this to be over, the whole weight of it, and she wanted that want to be respectable.

At a red light in a town with one intersection, his phone buzzed. Mika: "You coming Tuesday? Ryder got tickets." Then, before he could answer: "Also I found the thing from psych. Stroebe and Schut. It's called the dual process model. Look it up." Seth typed the names into the search bar while the light held. The screen told him that grieving people move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction. He read it twice. It was not advice about permission or courage; it was a description, like a map of weather. Oscillation, one site called it, though that word sat oddly, too tidy for the way his chest had loosened at a movie and tightened on the walk home.

He scrolled further, almost hoping the map would tell him which direction he was supposed to prefer, and of course it did not. That was the part he could not resolve, sitting in the parking lot of a gas station while his mother went in for coffee: whether facing the loss was the truer work and the rebuilding a kind of betrayal, or whether the rebuilding was the truer work and the grief a kind of vanity. Grandma's voice, gravelly, said something rude about the question itself. He put the phone face down on his knee and did not have an answer, and suspected the honest position was to hold both and admit it.

The lake when they reached it was flat and gray and exactly ordinary. His mother carried the box down the pebbled shore while Seth held the lid, because the lid did not fit well, and the wind was picking up. She started to say something formal, got two words in, and stopped. "She'd hate a speech," his mother said, and tipped the box, and a gust took some of the ash sideways onto Seth's sleeve, and he heard himself say, "She got you one last time," and his mother laughed, a real one, cracked open in the middle, and he laughed too, standing there with his grandmother on his jacket and his eyes wet.

On the drive back his phone buzzed again. He typed "yes" to Mika, then, before he could regret it, turned to his mother and said, "Tuesday, the late show, with Mika and Ryder. Is that okay." She looked at him for a long second and then reached over and turned the radio on, fiddling with the dial until she found the station Grandma used to argue with, and left it there, volume low, and drove.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow.
story:
Marcus set the staff paper on the kitchen table at eleven in the morning, when the house was still his, and pinned the corners down with two mugs and a fork. Sixteen bars. Four chords at least, changing. The assignment from Mr. Choi was the most concrete thing he had ever been handed, and also the most impossible, because it required him to decide, on purpose, what a melody should do.

He had started the night before with a rhythm, tapping it out on the table until his father had come down in socks and asked, not unkindly, whether the dishwasher had developed a fault. Now he tried the other way around, chords first. He wrote a G, then a C, then stared at the pencil as though it owed him money.

The phone buzzed. Aurelie had sent a photo of her own page, eight bars already filled, neat quarter notes marching like they knew where they were going. she's finished half already, the caption said, no punctuation, which was how Aurelie texted when she was gloating. Marcus turned the phone face down. He would not message Paxton for reassurance, because Paxton's reassurance, warm as it was, would only assuage him for about four minutes, and he had already used up this morning's four minutes twice.

Instead he hummed. He found a small phrase, five notes, and it didn't sound like much until he put a chord under it, and then it sounded like a question. He wrote it in the first bar, and it kept asking through the second and third, and by the fourth bar he understood that the notes were waiting for something the way he waited outside the auditorium last spring, listening to the jazz band tune up through the door.

Here was the problem. Sixteen bars was long. Halfway through, listeners would start to drift, would start folding their mental laundry the way Paxton did in assembly. Marcus needed something at the end of bar eight that would stop the drift, that would leave the listener leaning forward. He remembered Mr. Choi at the piano two weeks ago, playing two short phrases, the first one ending in a way that made the whole room hold still. "That one's a half cadence," Mr. Choi had said, fingers resting on the keys, and moved on before anyone could ask what he meant.

Marcus had no piano. He had the app on the tablet, which could play back anything he wrote in a voice like a polite ghost. He put a D major chord in bar eight, dominant, the fifth, the one his theory notebook marked with a single Roman numeral V, and played his eight bars through the tiny speaker. The phrase ended on that chord and it did not sound ended. It sounded like a hand held up, mid-sentence. He sat very still with his hand flat on the table, because a half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow, and that was exactly the trap door he had wanted under bar eight. Whoever heard it would have to keep listening to find out what came next. He would make them wait. He would make Aurelie wait.

He built the second half out of the same five-note question, turned upside down and slowed, so that the answer felt inevitable without being predictable, and at bar sixteen he landed hard on G major and let the ghost voice ring it out twice, the second time with a chord spelling mistake he fixed immediately, so no one would see it. Then he leaned back and read the whole thing the way Mr. Choi read, left to right, without stopping, and it held. It actually held.

That was when he heard the cough. Not from the hallway. From the window side of the room, faint, behind the steady noise of the neighbor's hedge trimmer, which had been going for twenty minutes and which was, he suddenly realized, not a hedge trimmer at all. He got up, crossed the kitchen, and pulled the curtain back from the side door. Mr. Choi was standing at his own patio table, ten feet away on the other side of the fence, headphones around his neck, a sandwich untouched beside him, and the fence between their yards was low enough that the polite ghost voice had been performing to an audience all morning.

"How long," Marcus said through the screen.

"Since the question in bar one," Mr. Choi said. He did not apologize. He picked up half the sandwich, a man not usually a gourmand but one who appreciated a meal with a score, and ate it slowly. "I was going to trim the hedge. Then you started humming."

Marcus felt his face go hot, the old atavistic urge to slam something, curtain or door, to make the listening stop. Instead he stood there, holding the curtain like a man deciding whether to open it wider. He thought of turning the page, of covering it, of the fact that Mr. Choi had heard every wrong chord he had tried and erased.

"Bar eight," Mr. Choi said. "You made us wait on purpose."

"Did it work?"

Mr. Choi put down the sandwich and looked at him across the low fence, and for a moment Marcus was certain he was about to grade it, out loud, in a yard, with mayo on his thumb. Instead Mr. Choi put the headphones back over his ears, picked up the trimmer, and said, "Play it again from the top. I missed bar twelve the first time."

Marcus went back to the table, set the tablet on the windowsill facing out, and pressed play.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
William had written the note three times in the margins of his biology notebook, and each version had sounded worse than the last. The first one, "Kyle's serve receive is killing us," was true but cruel. The second, "Maybe Kyle could work on passing," was kind but useless, so vague it could have meant anything. The third draft was just a question mark, which was honest in a way he hadn't intended.

The problem had started at Tuesday's practice, in the far corner of the gym where the light was worst and the balls came off the rafters at strange angles. Kyle had shanked four serves in a row, each one drifting left, and Coach had stopped the drill and asked the team, in that flat voice that meant he already knew, whether anyone had noticed a pattern. Nobody had said anything. Savanah had looked at her shoes. William had studied the dead spot on the ceiling tiles until Coach blew the whistle and moved on, and they had lost the scrimmage that followed by six points, mostly on balls Kyle never touched.

He was thinking about this now, sitting on the bleachers before Thursday's practice with his notebook open, supposedly reviewing morphology for the AP test. Savanah dropped down beside him with a paperback in her hand, its cover bent back so far it had learned a new shape.

"What's that?" William asked.

"My mom's book. She's making me read it for my internship." She held it up. Radical Candor, by Kim Scott. "It came out in 2017. It's about how to be a boss, but honestly it's just about telling people things."

William told her about Tuesday, about the silence, about the question mark in his notebook. He admitted the part he was least proud of, which was that he'd stayed quiet to be nice and it had cost them the scrimmage.

"That's the whole thing she's against," Savanah said, flipping to a dog-eared page. "Care personally and challenge directly. You have to do both, or it doesn't work." She read a few lines silently, then looked up. "Which one are you missing?"

He considered it. He cared about Kyle; they'd been friends since seventh grade, since the summer they'd both failed the deep-water test at the city pool and been put in the shallow group together. Caring wasn't the problem. "The second one, probably," he said, and it came out more like a guess than a conclusion, because he wasn't entirely sure. Maybe caring too much was the problem. Maybe they weren't separate things at all.

"If you only do the caring part," Savanah said, "she calls that ruinous empathy. You're nice to someone and you wreck them anyway." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it, and he had the feeling she was testing whether the phrase would land.

Practice began with passing drills, and Kyle predictably drifted to the back row, where shanked balls did the least damage. William found himself watching Kyle's feet instead of the ball, the way he rocked back onto his heels as the server tossed, weight settling wrong before anything else went wrong. It was like the morphology diagrams in his notebook, the ones that broke a cell into its parts and showed how shape followed function. Feet wide and staggered, platform early. Weight forward. It wasn't that Kyle couldn't pass. It was that his feet were telling a lie about where he thought the ball would go.

Between drills, William pulled out his phone and typed what he'd seen, then transcribed it onto a slip of scrap paper from Coach's clipboard table, editing as he went, crossing out "always" and "never," crossing out "terrible," which had snuck in despite everything. What remained was four sentences: when Kyle rocked onto his heels, the platform came up late and drifted left; when he stepped forward, the pass went flat and straight; he'd seen Kyle do it right at least a dozen times this season, including the dig against Riverside that had won the set.

He caught Kyle by the water cooler before the scrimmage. "Can I tell you something about serve receive? It might be wrong, but I've been watching."

Kyle wiped his mouth with his sleeve. "Sure."

"It's your heels. When you sit back on them, everything goes late and left. When you're forward, you're actually one of the best passers on the team. I'm not saying that to be nice. Riverside game, third set, you dug their captain flat."

Kyle was quiet long enough that William could hear the squeak of shoes on the far court. Then he said, "Coach said the same thing about my heels a month ago. I forgot."

"Why didn't you say anything Tuesday?"

"Why didn't you?" Kyle said, and it wasn't mean, just curious, the same tone William had used, and it occurred to him that the question was a fair one and that he didn't have an incisive answer to it, only the honest, unfinished one: he hadn't known yet how to say a hard thing without dropping it like a stone.

In the scrimmage, Kyle stepped forward on the first serve and passed it flat and perfect to Savanah, who set it to William for a kill. On the second serve Kyle rocked back again and shanked it left, and he looked over at William and shrugged, and William shrugged back, because one correction was not the same as a cure, and both of them seemed to understand that. The third serve, Kyle's feet were early. The pass was beautiful.

Afterward, in the parking lot while they waited for rides, William asked Savanah whether she thought the book's idea really worked in practice, or whether it only worked in offices where people got paid to be honest. She said she didn't know, that she'd only ever used it on her little brother, and that it had gone badly, and then, less badly.

"Less badly is something," William said.

"Less badly is most things," she said, and tossed him the paperback. "Keep it. Mom has three copies."

He turned it over in his hands, noting the creases in the spine, the chapters other hands had opened most. On Monday, he decided, he'd watch the heels again.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Florida Straits and north along the east coast of the United States.
story:
The trail climbed through pines above the visitor center, and Raphael carried the laminated current map rolled in his back pocket like a diploma he hadn't earned yet. In two hours Mr. Anderson expected him at the science museum downstairs, standing beside the wall-sized version of the same map, explaining to a room of ninth graders why Lisbon winters were milder than New York's. He had volunteered for this in a moment of ambition he now regarded the way one regards a tattoo chosen at fifteen.

"Tell me again why we're rehearsing on a mountain," Hala said, walking a few steps ahead with the confidence of someone who had never once mispronounced anything in public.

"Because if I do it outside, with distractions, the actual room will feel easy." Raphael had read this somewhere, possibly on a website that also sold protein powder.

Phoebe, the most phlegmatic of the three, stopped at a switchback and took out a granola bar. "Distract him, then," she said. "I'll be a ninth grader. I'm going to be unbearable." She adopted an expression of total vacancy, which, worryingly, suited her.

Raphael unrolled the map against a boulder and weighted the corners with pinecones. The Atlantic lay flat and blue, covered in arrows, warm currents drawn red and cold ones blue, and he understood the colors and nothing else. At school Mr. Anderson had given them one class period with the map and then asked for volunteers, and Raphael had raised his hand before he could lose his nerve, and Mr. Anderson had said only, "Make sure you can trace it from the beginning." Not which beginning. Not what it was called. Mr. Anderson taught by withholding, which he called inquiry and the students called annoying.

"Okay," Raphael said. "So. There's this current." He put his finger on the map and stopped. "It starts... somewhere."

"Bold opening," said Hala.

"Shut up. It's the Gulf Stream, right? The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current, that part I know. And it flows out of the Gulf of Mexico." He traced his finger from the wide pocket of water between Mexico and Florida. "Through the Florida Straits." His finger moved through the narrow channel between the peninsula and Cuba, out into the open Atlantic. "And then north along the east coast of the United States." He dragged his finger up past the Carolinas, and it was strange, he thought, how the line felt like the coastline's shadow, running parallel, stubborn, all the way up toward Newfoundland before it finally bent east.

Phoebe, still in character, said, "Cool. Why does that matter?" and bit her granola bar.

"That's the part I'm shaky on." He had half a page of notes about northern Europe, about Britain and Norway being warmer than their latitude deserved, and he believed it, mostly, but the chain between his finger and a mild January in Bergen had gaps he couldn't fill. He could say the current carried warmth north; he could not entirely say how that warmth got handed off to the wind, whether the ocean warmed the air or the air just happened to pass over, whether the map's red arrows meant temperature or something older and more technical. Two nights of reading had given him two vocabularies, one from a textbook and one from a fisherman's forum he'd found at midnight, and they disagreed about almost everything except the arrows themselves.

"Maybe don't claim more than the map shows," Hala said, and it was the first useful thing she'd offered. "You trace it, you say what it is, you say where it goes. If a kid asks you why Scotland has palm trees, you say that's a good question and you're not sure."

"Scotland has palm trees?"

"Four of them. In someone's yard. It was a whole article."

Raphael looked at his finger, still resting where the current bent away from America toward Europe. Mr. Anderson would hate the shrugging answer; Mr. Anderson wanted him to trace it from the beginning, and he could do that now, had done it, could do it again with a room watching. But the honest thing, the thing he was slowly deciding to build the talk around, was that the map showed him the where and not the why, and that a person could stand in front of an audience and say both. That was allowed. That might even be the whole job. He rolled the map tight again.

They reached the summit as the clouds thinned, and Phoebe produced a second granola bar from nowhere, revealing herself as a true gourmand of the trail. "One more time," she said, mouth full. "From the beginning. I'll be nice this time."

Raphael cleared his throat. "The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current," he said, "and it flows out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Florida Straits and north along the east coast of the United States."

"Now the hard part," said Hala.

"I know." He started down the trail, map in his fist. "Let me tell you what I don't know first."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state.
story:
Noemie counted the tomatoes twice before she let herself believe it: eleven, all still green, clustered on the two plants she and Maelie had staked in April. The community garden behind the shuttered textile mill had been her idea, technically, though Maelie had done most of the paperwork and Sahib had dragged the water barrels over from his uncle's restaurant. Now it was late July, and the well the gardeners shared was running low, and tonight there would be a meeting under the poplars to decide who got how much.

"They'll ration it," Maelie said, snapping a beetle off a leaf and flicking it into the grass. "Mr. Szabó already told my mom. First the plot holders with seniority, then the rest of us." She wiped her hands on her shorts. "The ones with seniority are the ones with the hoses."

Noemie knelt in the dirt and pressed a finger into the soil around the tomato roots. Dry. Not dusty yet, not the pale crumble that meant a plant had hours left, but dry in the way that would desiccate the lower leaves by Friday if the sky kept refusing to rain. She thought about the mill, how it had emptied in her grandmother's time and taken the wages with it, and how the empty lots had sat cracked and useless until someone decided food could grow there. Everything in this garden seemed to have a history behind it like that, a decision made somewhere else that arrived here as weather or soil or a locked gate.

At the meeting, folding chairs wobbled on the packed earth. The plot holders argued in the overlapping way of people who all believed they were being reasonable. An older woman in a straw hat said she'd grown vegetables on this land since before the fountain plaza was a parking lot, and the parking lot had raised the temperature of the whole block, which was why everything dried out faster now, though she didn't put it exactly that way; she put it as a complaint about asphalt. Sahib's uncle's cousin, who managed the restaurant, said food waste from the kitchens could be composted here if someone hauled it, and hauling cost money, and money was a thing the garden had never had. Mr. Szabó, who kept bees at the far fence and wore the same grey shirt in every season like a man of ascetic habits, mostly listened. When someone asked him directly, he only said, "The bees find water. I don't."

Noemie had come with something prepared. In the spring, Mr. Szabó's copy of a environmental history reader had sat open on the bench by the hives, and she had read a page while waiting for Maelie, and then read it again at home because it seemed impossible. She stood up when the argument about seniority circled back a third time.

"The 1987 Montreal Protocol," she said, and heard her voice go flat the way it did when she was nervous, "phases out ozone-destroying chemicals. It was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state." She paused. Someone's chair creaked. "Every one. I looked it up because I didn't believe it."

"That's chemicals, not water," the woman in the straw hat said, but not unkindly.

"I know. I'm not saying it's the same." Noemie felt Maelie watching her from the second row. "I used to think nobody agrees on anything that costs them something. My mom says that about the rent negotiations at her building. But that protocol, they all ratified it, and it cost them something. So it's not that agreement is impossible. It's that it's rare, and I don't know what makes it happen." She looked down at her notes, which said only: barrels, schedule, Montreal. "I'm proposing we stop arguing seniority and write a rotation. Everyone signs it. If one person cheats, the whole thing breaks, and everyone knows that, so maybe that's why they'd sign."

They argued about it for forty more minutes. Sahib volunteered to chart the rotation on graph paper, and the aesthete in him came out as he did it, ruling the lines with a straightedge and insisting the columns be evenly spaced, the names in blue and the days in black. The woman in the straw hat gave up her Tuesday slot in exchange for a say in where the compost bins went. A man who had spoken sharply about freeloaders left early without signing, and his plot was the one nearest the tap.

Walking home along the mill fence, Noemie and Maelie passed under the poplars, their leaves turning silver-side-out in the evening wind. Maelie kicked a bottle cap into the gutter.

"You think he'll sign," she said. Not a question.

"I think the tomatoes need water by Friday either way," Noemie said.

They stopped at the corner where the streetlights began. Behind them the garden lay in shadow except for the glass of Mr. Szabó's hive boxes catching the last light, and somewhere near the tap, the unsigned man was standing at his plot with a hose, watering in the dark.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Aristotle held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary.
story:
The radiator next to the window ticked like something counting down, and Leo copied the date into his notebook without thinking about it. Ms. Haile was writing on the board in her narrow, tilted hand: voluntary, involuntary, force, ignorance of the circumstances. "Aristotle," she said, "held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily. And that actions done under force, or through ignorance of the circumstances, can be involuntary." She set the marker down. "That's the whole claim. Now somebody give me a case."

Aleksander, two seats over, kept his eyes on his desk. Leo noticed this because Aleksander never kept his eyes on his desk; he usually argued about everything, loudly, half to annoy Soren and half because he seemed to enjoy the sound of his own reasoning. Today he was drawing a small igneous-looking rock in the margin of his notes, shading it in careful layers, as if he were some aesthete with no stake in the discussion, which Leo knew he was not.

The case was already in the room. Last week Aleksander had told Soren, in the parking lot where half the class could hear, that a girl on the swim team had been seen leaving a hotel with the assistant coach. He said he'd heard it from his cousin. Soren had repeated it at lunch, and by Friday the girl's mother had called the school, and the assistant coach had cleared it up in an afternoon, because he had been at a funeral with his sister, receipts and all. The girl had come back to school on Monday and sat alone in every class, and nobody had apologized, because nobody was sure who had started it, and nobody wanted to be the first to admit a part in it.

Soren raised his hand. "What if somebody does something bad but doesn't know it's bad? Like they pass something on that turns out to be false."

"That's a case," Ms. Haile said. "Whose is it?"

"Nobody's," Soren said. "Hypothetical."

"Fine. Keep it hypothetical." She sat on the edge of her desk, which she did when she wanted them to forget she was grading them. "So the question becomes whether the person acted through ignorance of the circumstances. And then, whether that makes it involuntary. Work in pairs. Ten minutes."

Leo turned his chair toward Aleksander, because they were seated alphabetically and because Aleksander was closest and because Leo wanted to watch his face. "You heard it from your cousin," Leo said. "You didn't know it was false."

"I didn't," Aleksander said. His pencil stopped on the rock. "So I'm not responsible. That's the whole argument. Voluntary means you know what you're doing. I didn't know."

"But you chose to say it in the parking lot where everyone could hear." Leo kept his voice level, the way his father did when negotiating with the insurance company, matter-of-fact, no heat. "The choosing part was voluntary. The false part you couldn't help."

"That's two actions," Aleksander said. "Aristotle would say only one of them counts against me."

"Would he? Or is that just you, splitting it up so the part you're guilty of gets smaller?" Leo watched him. It was strange how people could externalize like that, push the blame out of themselves and onto the cousin, the parking lot, the acoustics, until the whole thing was just weather that had happened to occur.

Aleksander looked at him for a long moment. "Soren's the one who repeated it at lunch," he said finally. "In front of her friends."

"Soren heard it from you."

"That's what I mean. It's a chain. Nobody's at the start of it."

"Your cousin's at the start of it."

"My cousin heard it from somebody."

Ms. Haile called the room back together. When the bell rang she held Aleksander's eye for a second longer than usual, no accusation in it, just attention, and Aleksander packed up fast and left without the usual argument about the homework. Soren lingered, zipping and unzipping his bag, and then said, to nobody in particular, "I'm going to tell her I'm sorry. Not because of the philosophy. Just because she sat alone all week."

Leo walked out behind him into the corridor, where the floors had just been mopped and smelled of industrial lemon. He still didn't know where the line fell, whether a bad act with an unknown false core counted against Aleksander at half weight or full weight or none, and he suspected Aristotle had left that part for people to fight about on purpose. But the choosing was real, and Aleksander knew it, whatever he said about his cousin. At the end of the hall the girl from the swim team was at her locker, and Soren stopped in front of her and put his bag down on the floor.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Progressive overload means gradually increasing training demands, such as weight, distance or intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt.
story:
The track behind the school had a long puddle at the second curve that never dried, even in June, and Rosalie had learned to run the outside lane there as though the lane itself were impermeable to her. She stood at the start line with a notebook in her hand, which was unusual for her, because for three years she had kept everything in her head. The notebook was new. The plan inside it was newer.

For most of the summer she had run the same thing every day: six laps, fast enough to hurt, then home. When the season's first time trial came, she was three seconds slower than her spring time. She had assumed effort accumulated like coins in a jar. Now, on the advice of nobody in particular, she was trying to write down a week on paper, with boxes for each day, and she kept arriving at the same problem. Every time she drew the grid, she wanted to fill all seven boxes with work, and some stubborn voice said that a day of nothing was a day wasted, that rest was for people who didn't want it badly enough.

Martha arrived at five past six, the way she always did, hair still wet from the shower, apologizing in advance for whatever she was about to do badly. Martha's event was the eight hundred, and for four months she had run the identical workout every Tuesday and Thursday: eight repeats of two hundred metres, ninety seconds of standing rest between each, no more, no less. She was diligent about it, almost ceremonially so, and she was still a full second off the personal best she'd set in February. She wanted that second the way some people want an apology, and she had begun to talk about it the way people talk about the weather, as a condition that simply existed.

"You could look at what you wrote down," Sidney said, sprawled on the infield with one shoe off, inspecting a blister. Sidney had come out for the team in the spring mostly, Rosalie suspected, because the warm-up lap was twenty minutes of uninterrupted talking, and Sidney was a natural raconteur who could turn a trip to the dentist into a three-act story with a false ending. "Write it down and I can't argue with you. That's the whole point of paper."

"I'm not writing it down so you'll stop arguing."

"You could, though. As a side benefit."

Rosalie crouched on the track with the notebook flat on her thigh and asked Martha to describe the Tuesday workout again, and Martha did, and Rosalie heard it with a strange new attention, the way you hear a word repeated until it loses its shape. Four months. The same eight repeats. The same rest. Her own six laps every day. It was as if both of them had been paying the same instalment over and over, expecting the debt to shrink, as though effort could be amortized by repetition alone, the same payment applied to the same balance forever. Somewhere she had half-remembered a line from a clinic pamphlet she'd read in a waiting room, and now the phrase surfaced whole: progressive overload. She said it out loud, experimentally, and Martha stopped stretching and looked at her.

"What's that mean, you add something? Like weight, or distance, or you go harder?"

"Yeah," Rosalie said, slowly, because she was assembling it as she spoke. "Gradually. So your body keeps having a reason to adapt." She looked down at her grid of seven empty boxes. If the demands never changed, there was no reason for anything to change. If they changed too fast, there was injury. Somewhere between was a shape she couldn't see yet, and she had the sudden, uncomfortable sense that her old instinct, more every day, all seven boxes, was not ambition but a kind of illiteracy about her own body. She thought of February, of Martha's old best, of how they had both assumed that stopping was the same as failing.

Mr. Diallo, who lived in the house that backed onto the track and ran before work in a faded marathon shirt from a city neither of them could identify, slowed to a walk as he passed them. "You two are here early," he said, not a question, and Martha asked him, in the blunt way she asked things, whether he ever took days off. He said every Monday and every Sunday, that he'd tried otherwise at her age and spent a season hurt, and then he was gone down the curve, around the puddle, waving once without turning.

Rosalie drew a hard line through Sunday and wrote nothing in it. Under Monday she wrote an easy three laps, and after Tuesday's repeats she added, next to Martha's familiar eight, a small note: ten next week, or two hundred and fifty each, decide Monday. Martha leaned over her shoulder to read it and didn't say anything for a moment, which for Martha was a long time. "I've been doing the same thing since the ice was on the track," she said, mostly to the infield. Sidney sat up and put the shoe back on. Rosalie turned to a fresh page, laid the pen against the top line, and said, "Okay. Tell me the eight hundred again, from the start."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level.
story:
Kayla's essay prompt sat open on her laptop like an accusation: compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government. Her father had promised to drive her to the library before it closed, but his shift ran long, so she was home with her mother's old politics textbook, a bag of frozen peas pressed against her swollen jaw where the wisdom teeth had come out two days before, and the clock. Draft due Monday.

She had the easy half done. Presidential: the people, indirectly through an electoral college in the American case, choose a president for a fixed term, and removal requires impeachment, a bar deliberately set so high that it almost never clears. Parliamentary was murkier. The legislature picks the prime minister; the legislature can also unmake one. That much she understood. What she could not figure out was how a country avoided collapsing into chaos if a government could fall at any moment, and every search seemed to exhume the same dry procedural language from websites that looked like they had been built in 2003.

She texted Kimberly, who had the same class. Kimberly texted back a shrug emoji and then, three minutes later, "wait, are you doing Germany? Mr. Lawson told my brother Germany has this weird rule where they can't just vote no, they have to vote yes to somebody new." Kayla frowned at her phone. Vote yes to somebody new. She typed Helmut Schmidt into the search bar, because if there was a rule, there had to be a time it was used.

The result rearranged something in her head. In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence. She read the sentence twice, mouthing it around the peas. A chancellor, gone, replaced, with no general election at all. The German people had never voted for Kohl that year; the parliament had simply decided. And it was the only time the procedure had ever succeeded at the federal level. Only once, in all the decades. Which meant the mechanism existed mostly as a threat, a door that stayed locked because everyone knew where the key hung.

She called Kimberly, who picked up on the second ring, sounding like she was eating cereal. "Okay, so I found it," Kayla said. "It's called a constructive vote of no confidence." She spelled constructive for her, and Kimberly said, "Constructive like you have to build the new government before you knock down the old one," which was not quite the technical phrasing but close enough that Kayla laughed and then winced because laughing hurt.

Louis-Philippe, who was doing the American half of the comparison, joined their group chat and immediately complicated everything. He argued that the fixed presidential term was a virtue, that stability mattered more than responsiveness, that you should not be able to swap leaders midstream the way Germany had. Kayla sat with the cursor blinking and found herself arguing the other side without quite having decided to. If a prime minister loses the confidence of parliament, she typed, the system corrects itself in days, not after a two-year lame duck. He countered that the German way meant a handful of legislators could undo what voters had chosen. Both of them were right, she realized, in the way that made essays hard.

She heard the front door, then her father's keys in the bowl, and the particular quiet of him noticing the kitchen light on and not calling out. He appeared in her doorway with a glass of applesauce, because she still could not chew, and set it beside her laptop without being asked. "How's it going?" he said. She told him about Kohl and Schmidt, 1982, the only time it had worked at the federal level, and he said, "Huh, I didn't know that," which felt like a small trophy.

Later, near midnight, she had two paragraphs that held both perspectives at once, an old adage about not letting the perfect defeat the good floating uselessly at the top of her draft until she cut it. What she could not resolve, she left unresolved on purpose: a paragraph that said, plainly, that she could not say which system was more democratic, only that they distributed the risk differently. She read it over, decided it was either the most honest thing she had written or the biggest dodge of her young academic career, and printed it anyway. The printer ground and hesitated like it was shaping something igneous out of the dark, and then the pages slid warm into her hand, and she squared their edges against the desk and turned off the lamp.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
David had ruined the chair four times by Sunday afternoon. The assignment from Ms. Pérez was a charcoal drawing of a single object, rendered from life, due Tuesday, and he had chosen the kitchen chair because it was the nearest thing to him when she asked. Now the chair sat on the table's far end like an accusation while he worked at the near end with his sketchbook, a kneaded eraser going gray in his fingers, and a row of crumpled attempts on the floor beside him.

The problem was the legs. He could draw the seat as a slab, the back as a grid of rungs, but where the legs joined the seat the lines went soft and wrong, and the whole structure tilted like something about to slide out from under an invisible person. He had tried starting with the seat and moving down. He had tried measuring with his pencil at arm's length, the way Ms. Pérez had demonstrated, counting heads and halves. Each drawing looked plausible for ten minutes and then revealed itself as a chair that could not stand.

His mother came through for tea while he was on the fourth attempt. She was recuperating from a cold she refused to admit had been serious, wrapped in the gray cardigan she wore only when unwell, and she stood behind him long enough to sip once. "It looks fine," she said, in the tone she used when she meant she did not want to discourage him. "The legs are a bit thin."

"They're the wrong thin," David said. She touched his shoulder and went upstairs.

Alessandra arrived at six with her own sketchbook under her arm and half a bag of pistachios. She had drawn a pair of hiking boots and considered herself finished, which was typical, and she sat down across from him and shelled nuts while he started the fifth chair. When it failed the same way, she leaned over the table and looked not at his drawing but at the chair itself.

"You're staring at the legs," she said. "Draw the holes instead."

"What holes?"

"The gaps. Between the legs, under the seat, around the rungs. It's called negative space. The empty area around and between the subjects." She turned her sketchbook over and drew a quick frame, then the shapes of nothing, the window-like openings framed by the chair's structure, and where she finished, the chair's outline appeared on its own, correct without ever having been drawn directly.

"That's a trick," David said.

"It's the same chair," Alessandra said. "You're just looking at the part you keep getting wrong by getting everything else right."

He did not believe her, exactly. He believed her drawing, which was the thing he could not argue with, but it felt like cheating, like being handed the answer to something he wanted to solve himself. His father had a version of this argument that came up whenever the subject of art school did: that drawing was not a trade, that a person needed solvency first and self-expression after, that talent was fine but talent did not pay for a flat. David had been building a private case against that view all year, and privately he had adopted its opposite, that the honest way was to look directly at the thing itself and fight it line by line until the lines obeyed. Drawing the emptiness instead felt like a retreat.

But the emptiness was not empty. He took a fresh sheet and squinted past the chair until the wood went dark and shapeless and only the openings between the legs stood out, pale and flat, like holes cut in the paper. He drew those shapes and nothing else: the tall gap under the seat, the trapezoids between the legs, the squares framed by the back rungs. When he stepped back, the chair was there, and the legs, which he had never once drawn, were right. He sat down again and looked at it for a long moment. It was still the same looking. He had simply stopped deciding in advance what counted as the subject.

Lucca texted at eight to ask if David had finished, and David sent him a photo of the sheet. Lucca replied with three fire emojis and the message "since when are you good at legs." Alessandra ate the last pistachio and said his mother should come see it, and David said she was asleep, and then he heard her on the stairs in the cardigan, coming down for more tea.

He turned the drawing toward the door before she reached the kitchen.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Kazuo Ishiguro's 1989 novel The Remains of the Day, the butler Stevens reports events accurately but misreads their meaning, including his own feelings.
story:
Zachary had read the same page four times before he noticed what was bothering him. The butler, Stevens, described the evening his father died. He described the dinner service he was running at the same time, the guests downstairs, the trays of food, and then he wrote that he had felt a sense of triumph at having carried off the evening so smoothly. Zachary set the book on his knee. Was that what triumph felt like? His own father had once stood in the doorway of the kitchen after Zachary's grandmother's funeral, still in his tie, eating cold rice out of a container, and had said nothing at all.

He carried the book to the kitchen where his mother was sorting mail at the counter. "Can you be proud of something and sad about it at the same time?" he asked.

"That's a strange question for a Tuesday," she said, not looking up. "Yes."

"But if someone only told you the proud part. Only told you the triumph part." He turned the book over in his hands. "Would you believe them?"

She set a bill down and looked at him properly then. "Is this about Landyn?"

"No. It's homework." He went back upstairs, though the question about Landyn stayed with him, because Landyn had sworn last month that he was fine, absolutely fine, about being cut from the team, and then had not answered texts for nine days.

Ms. Nakamura had assigned them The Remains of the Day, 1989, Ishiguro, and had written one sentence on the board before class ended: "Consider what the narrator tells you and what he shows you." She had refused to say more. She was obstreperous that way, cheerful and immovable, and when Daphnee had asked her directly whether Stevens was lying, she had said, "Read the chapter again and tell me tomorrow," which had made Daphnee throw her hands up.

Zachary texted Daphnee now. "Is Stevens lying about the father thing?"

"Define lying," she wrote back. He could picture her at her own desk, highlighters lined up like surgical instruments.

"He says he felt triumphant. But who feels triumphant when their dad dies? He doesn't miss a single course at dinner. He's like a stoic, he just keeps serving."

"Maybe he is lying."

But Zachary didn't think it was that simple, and the simplicity bothered him the way a wrong answer on a test bothers you before you know it's wrong. Stevens reported the facts perfectly. The time of death, the arrangements made, the service completed. Every detail checked out. It was the meaning of the details that had gone sideways somewhere. Zachary got a clean sheet of paper and drew a line down the middle. On the left he wrote WHAT HE SAYS HE FELT. On the right he wrote WHAT HE DID. Under the second column, after the father's death, he wrote: served dinner, felt triumph, mentions waiting years later to think about it. He underlined the last phrase twice, because people who genuinely feel triumphant don't usually announce that they'll reflect on it later, the way people who aren't hurt don't need to say they're fine.

He called Landyn. It rang six times.

"Hey," Landyn said. His voice was flat, careful.

"Are you fine?" Zachary asked. "Actually fine?"

There was a pause long enough that Zachary could hear a television somewhere in the background. "I'm doing homework," Landyn said.

"Okay. Because Stevens keeps saying he's fine too, and he's not, and I can tell because of what he does, not what he says. So I'm checking yours."

Another pause. "You're checking whether I'm an unreliable narrator."

"Basically, yeah."

Landyn laughed once, a real one, surprised out of him. "I maybe sublimate a little. Coach says I put everything into the rowing machine." It was true; Landyn had been on the erg in the school gym every evening that week, another fact Zachary had collected without thinking of it as evidence.

They talked for twenty minutes about nothing important after that, and when Zachary hung up, the sheet of paper was still on his desk, the two columns sitting side by side like accounts that wouldn't reconcile. He wasn't sure yet what to write in his essay. Stevens misread his own feelings, that much Zachary believed, and he also believed a person could report events accurately and still get the truth wrong, which was stranger and more interesting than lying. What he couldn't decide was whether that made Stevens a man to distrust or a man to feel sorry for, or whether those were the same thing.

He picked up the pen, and at the bottom of the page, beneath both columns, he wrote: "Trust the actions. Question the rest." Then he crossed out "Question the rest" and sat looking at the blank space where it had been, the pen still in his hand, the lamp humming over the open book.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Hayden had signed up to walk dogs at the Riverside Animal Shelter because the court of college applications demanded forty hours of service, and the shelter was close enough to reach by bicycle. He arrived on a grey Saturday expecting the smell of bleach and the sound of barking, and he got both, but he also got Mr. Goh, the shelter manager, who met him at the door with an apologetic tilt of his head. A pipe had burst in the kennel wing. The dogs were crated in the offices, the walking paths were torn up, and there was nothing for a volunteer to do but go home, unless. Unless, Mr. Goh said, he didn't mind carrying boxes, because the food bank shared the building's rear warehouse, and Saturday was their heaviest morning.

Hayden followed him down a corridor past the cat rooms, through a door with a hand-lettered sign, and into a warehouse so tall that his footsteps sounded borrowed. Two teenagers he recognized from school, Elsa and Easton, were already stacking canned goods on folding tables, and a queue of people waited outside the loading bay with laundry baskets and wheeled carts. Elsa waved him over and put a clipboard in his hands. His job was to transcribe the intake numbers from each donation box onto a sheet, because the woman who normally did it was out sick and the numbers had to go somewhere.

He worked through the morning, and it was fine, and then it was not fine. A man near the front of the queue, holding a child's hand, was told that the formula he needed was out of stock, and Hayden watched the man's shoulders lower by a full inch. There was no scene. The man nodded, took what he could, and left, and the line closed over the gap he left behind as though he had never stood there. Hayden wrote 14 on the clipboard and hated the number a little. Beside him, Easton said the whole system was broken, that food banks shouldn't have to exist at all, that charity was a bandage over something deleterious and structural, and he said it with the certainty of someone who had recently learned the word for it.

Elsa, sorting rice with quick hands, said that was easy to say when you'd never missed a meal. Easton said she was missing the point. They went back and forth in the low, careful voices people use when they are arguing in front of strangers, and Hayden, who agreed with parts of both and all of neither, said nothing. During a lull he drifted to the warehouse wall, where a poster hung crooked beside the fire extinguisher. St. Mary's Food Bank, Phoenix, Arizona, it read, the world's first food bank, founded in 1967 by a man named John van Hengel. He read it twice. A first. Somewhere, someone had invented this, the queue, the clipboard, the numbers, and everything since had been a descendent of that one warehouse in the desert.

"Did you know there was a first one?" he asked Elsa when she came over with an empty bin. "This whole thing, it started with one guy in 1967. John van Hengel, in Phoenix."

"So it's not inevitable," she said, resting the bin on her hip. "Somebody chose it."

"Yeah," Hayden said. "But Easton's also right that somebody chose the other thing too." He looked at his clipboard, at the column of numbers he had made, at the line outside where a woman was counting cans into a bag before she even reached her car. He had come here for the dogs, to be honest, and instead he was standing in the middle of an argument much older than his morning, and he could feel both sides of it in his hands.

He caught up with Easton by the loading bay during the last hour. "I'm not saying you're wrong," Hayden said. "About the structure. I think you're mostly right. I just keep thinking about that guy in Phoenix. He couldn't fix anything either. He just made a place." Easton considered this while sliding a crate of apples across the tailgate of a van. "A place isn't nothing," he admitted, which for Easton was practically litotes, and Hayden laughed and said he didn't think that word meant what Easton kept using it to mean, and Elsa, passing with a dolly, called out that neither of them knew what any words meant.

The warehouse emptied by two. Mr. Goh appeared in the doorway to say the pipe was fixed and the dogs would need walkers tomorrow, and Hayden said he'd come, but he asked first whether the food bank needed anyone on Saturdays, regularly, numbers and boxes. Mr. Goh said he'd introduce him to the coordinator. Outside, Hayden unlocked his bicycle and stood a moment in the cold, unsure whether forty hours had become four hundred or whether he was only promising himself something easy, the way people do after a day that moved them. Across the lot, Elsa and Easton were still arguing, walking side by side toward the bus stop, and Elsa looked back and called, "You're on intake next week, so learn the alphabet."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer.
story:
Vincent had signed up for the summer critique class at the community art studio because it was free and air-conditioned, in that order, and he had not expected the first assignment to be Frida Kahlo. Mr. Siddiqui had pinned a print of The Broken Column to the corkboard and said, "Formal analysis only, people. Colour, composition, symbolism. No biographies, no feelings, no 'relatability.' Two pages, Friday." Lewis, sitting cross-legged on the paint-spattered floor, raised his hand and asked whether "no feelings" was itself a feeling, and Mr. Siddiqui said that was a detentionable thought in a building that had no detentions.

The trouble was that Vincent kept having feelings anyway. He came back to the studio on Wednesday evening to look again, mostly because Alexe had said she'd be there practicing her charcoal, and partly because the painting had done something to him he could not file. Nails pierce the figure's face and body in the image, and tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer. That was the part that undid him. Suffering, he could sort into categories. Suffering that watches you back was a different taxonomic problem.

"You're staring at her like she owes you money," Alexe said, not looking up from her charcoal.

"She's staring at me like I owe her money," Vincent said. "I'm trying to write about composition and I can't look at her eyes for more than four seconds. I did experiments. Four seconds, then I have to check the exit."

"That's the whole point, though. That's her being brave." Alexe frowned at her paper. "That's what my critique says. 'The direct gaze demonstrates courage.'"

Vincent wanted to argue and was annoyed to find he half-agreed, which was the most pugnacious possible mood, arguing with a position you were already losing to. "But that's exactly what Mr. Siddiqui said not to do. That's biography leaking in. That's us deciding she's brave because we want her to be." He flipped his notebook open to a page of abandoned half-sentences. "I wrote 'the tears use a cool palette that rhymes with the sky' and then I wrote 'why does the sky get to rhyme.' I'm not well, Alexe."

Lewis arrived carrying two iced teas and a theory. "Okay so hear me out. The eyes are a formal element. A line goes out of the painting, from her to us. Mr. Siddiqui can't ban lines. He banned feelings, not geometry." He distributed the teas with the gravity of a man settling estates. "Vincent, you write it as, 'the gaze constructs the viewer's position within the composition,' and then you're a genius instead of a person who got uncomfortable."

"That's cowardice with a thesaurus," Alexe said.

"It's phenomenology," Lewis said, pleased with himself. "Which is cowardice with a thesaurus, but published."

Vincent laughed, then stopped laughing, because something slotted into place. He pulled his notebook over and wrote fast before the thought could escape into the humid air. The nails made you want to look away; the tears made you sorry for looking; and the gaze straight at the viewer made you unable to do either. That was the composition doing the work. The painting was not telling him she was brave. It was making him feel caught, and he had been trying to name the feeling instead of describing the mechanism that produced it. He read his own paragraph back and found, with some relief, that it allayed the thing he'd been carrying all week, that itch of looking away and not knowing why.

Friday, Mr. Siddiqui read the critiques aloud, anonymous, a ritual he performed like a man reading entrails. When he reached Vincent's, he paused at the sentence about the gaze pinning the viewer between pity and flight, and read it twice. "This one," he said, "has the only paragraph in the stack that does not tell me how Kahlo felt. It tells me what the painting does. Excellent." There was a beat of silence in which Vincent tried very hard to look like a person who had not written that.

Then Mr. Siddiqui turned the page. "Although the final line, 'and maybe she is brave, I honestly can't tell from inside the painting, and I think that not being able to tell is the point,' loses a mark for hedging."

Vincent kept his face neutral while Lewis leaned over and whispered, "You hedged. Beautifully. Like a rosebush." Alexe passed him a folded note that said, I still think she's brave, and underneath, in smaller letters, but your way of not knowing is better than my way of knowing.

At the end of class Mr. Siddiqui rolled the print down off the corkboard and handed it, unexpectedly, to Vincent. "Hang it back up for me. Careful with the pins." Vincent pressed the first pin into the cork, and the print's eyes met his, steady, tear-streaked, punctured, and refusing to blink. He held it there for a long moment. "Four and a half seconds," he told her. "New record."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
The tour guide walked backward the whole time, which Jacob found either impressive or alarming, and he hadn't decided which. "This is Whitmore Hall," she announced, gesturing at a building that looked like a brick had married a spaceship. "Housing, classrooms, and the office where you'll spend your happiest and saddest hours, depending on your financial aid."

Jacob raised his hand before he could stop himself. "Is the aid part of the application, or separate?"

"FAFSA," said a girl near him, not unkindly, before the guide could answer. "It's its own form. My mom and I did ours at one in the morning last week."

"You did the what?"

"The FAFSA. It's the form everyone fills out for federal financial aid, like Pell Grants and loans. And the state uses it, and the college uses it too, for their own money." She said it fast, the way you recite something you've recited forty times. "I'm Simona, by the way."

"Jacob." He filed the word away like a receipt he was afraid of losing. Nobody at his school had mentioned any form. His father had said, more than once, that money was a solved problem, that they would manage, that Jacob's job was simply to get in. His mother, by contrast, kept a binder of scholarship printouts and a calculator on the kitchen counter, and referred to the whole enterprise as "the siege." Two philosophies, and Jacob had been standing comfortably between them for months, doing nothing.

The tour moved on toward the library, and Simona fell into step beside him. "You really hadn't heard of it?"

"I thought admission was the whole battle."

"That's adorable," she said. "My mom made a spreadsheet with three tabs. There's a deadline for the state aid, so we were up late, me reading numbers off tax forms, her typing and swearing in two languages. It was almost fun, actually. Like a heist."

"Did it presage anything good?" Jacob asked, and immediately regretted it, because who talked like that. But Simona only squinted at him.

"Did it what?"

"Presage. Signal ahead of time. Whether the numbers meant you'd get anything."

"Oh. Then yes. It presaged a very small grant and a medium-sized loan." She grinned. "And a nap."

The guide had stopped beneath an elm tree to deliver a speech about tradition, and Jacob noticed, off to the side, a man in a lanyard herding a straggling parent. The lanyard man caught Jacob's eye and mouthed, "Backward walking is an artifice, don't be fooled," with the gravity of someone sharing state secrets. It took Jacob a moment to realize this was a joke, and by then the man had moved on, straight-backed, forward-walking, ordinary.

At the dining hall, the tour was released to eat and recover. Simona found a table with another classmate from the tour, a quieter girl named Kathryn, who was eating a sandwich with the focus of someone disassembling a bomb. When Jacob sat down, Kathryn looked up and said, "You're the one who asked about money."

"Is that bad?"

"It's the only sensible question anyone asked all morning. Everyone else wanted to know about the climbing wall." She set down the sandwich. "The climbing wall is an artifice. The whole tour is an artifice, honestly. I keep waiting for them to show us the room where they reject people."

"There's probably a museum," Simona said. "Very tasteful. Antiquated letter opener displayed under glass."

Jacob laughed, then found he couldn't stop talking. He told them about the binder, the siege, the solved problem, the two parents orbiting the same future from opposite directions. "My dad thinks talking about money jinxes the admission. My mom thinks not talking about it jinxes everything else. And I've been agreeing with both of them, which, I've started to notice, is just a fancy way of agreeing with nobody."

"So ask," Kathryn said.

"Ask who?"

"Whoever knows. Tonight. Before it's some state deadline and you're doing tax forms at one in the morning with a parent swearing bilingually."

Simona raised her plastic cup. "It was a good night. I recommend it to everyone."

He called his mother from the corner of the parking lot while the afternoon cooked itself down to gold. "FAFSA," he said. "Do we know about that?" There was a pause long enough that he could hear her turn a page in the binder. Then, strangely, a laugh.

"Your father said he handled it," she said. "He didn't, did he."

"I don't think so."

"Get in the car," she said, which Jacob understood to mean sit still, "and tell me everything that girl said." He relayed it: the form for federal aid, Pell Grants, loans, and the state and the colleges using it too, the deadlines, the one-in-the-morning. On the other end he heard a drawer open, the kitchen calculator being carried somewhere with purpose.

"Jacob," his mother said, "you realize you just did the thing you never do."

"What thing?"

"Something."

He looked back toward the quad, where the tour guide was walking a new group backward under the elms, arms wide, promising things. His father would say he had overstepped. His mother would say he had under-waited. Jacob thought the truth was that he had, for once, picked up the phone.

"Come home," his mother said. "We're doing forms tonight."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and old popcorn, and the eighth graders were already scatter-passing when Blake came in with his clipboard. He had spent two evenings designing the drills. The younger team could not pass under pressure; their weakness was specific and obvious, a hesitation before every release, the ball held a half-second too long while a defender closed. His plan was built around three-corner passing with a token chaser, and he believed in it the way you can only believe in something you made yourself.

"Watch this," he said to Parker, who had agreed to help for the period and was leaning against the bleachers with his arms crossed.

The drill worked, at first. The kids moved the ball in triangles, calling names, and when someone held on too long Blake blew the whistle and told him exactly what he had done wrong. Elbow lower. Eyes up sooner. He corrected every pass, every time, because that was what coaching looked like to him. That was what his own coaches had done, men whose voices he could still hear in his ears during layup lines years later.

Parker jogged the drill with them for ten minutes and then came back to the sideline, breathing hard. "You're talking after every single one," he said. "Like a pundit on a highlight show. Nonstop commentary."

"That's the job," Blake said. But he had noticed something too. The kids passed well only when he spoke. In the gaps between his corrections, the passes got sloppy again, and one boy, the smallest one, had started glancing at the sideline before releasing the ball, checking whether Blake had something to say.

Mr. Li, who taught physics and supervised the gym on Wednesdays, was folding the mats along the far wall. Blake had been half-conscious of him all afternoon. When the whistle drill ended and Mr. Li waved him over, Blake expected a speech and steeled himself for it. Instead Mr. Li asked whether the kids had tried the drill with him silent.
