"No," Blake said. "Why would they?"

"Try five minutes," Mr. Li said, and went back to his mats.

Blake called them in, told them the same drill, and then said nothing. It was harder than he expected. Every wobble of a pass pulled a sentence up into his throat, and he had to swallow it. The first minute was a mess, worse than before, and he felt his plan curdling. Then something shifted. The smallest boy, the one who had been checking the sideline, began correcting himself, saying "too slow" under his breath after a late release, and adjusting on the next pass. Two of the others started doing the same. The passing was rougher than it had been under his voice, but it was theirs.

At the water break Alana arrived early for open gym and sat down beside the score table. "You look like you got beaten by a drill," she said.

Blake told her about it, the whistle after every attempt, then the silence. "There's a name for it, I think," he said. "Mr. Li mentioned it before you got here. The guidance hypothesis. Feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it. Less frequent feedback helps retention." He had written it on the back of his clipboard in small letters, the way he wrote formulas he did not yet fully trust. "So every time I fixed them, I was teaching them to need me."

"That's depressing," Alana said.

"I don't know if it's that simple." He turned his clipboard over. "They got worse before they got better. In a game, worse might mean they stop trying. And some of them, the two smallest ones, they really did need every correction or the form fell apart completely." He was thinking of his own years on the receiving end of constant coaching, how much of it had made him better and how much of it had made him afraid to move without instruction. He could not separate the two now, and he suspected he never fully would.

The kids came back from the water fountain with their shoes squeaking on the polished floor, and the smallest one stopped in front of him, ball under his arm. "Are you going to talk this time or not?"

"Every fifth pass," Blake said, because it was the first thing that came to him, and it turned out to be a real decision, made in real time, the kind you could not predicate on any theory because it depended on ten specific boys on a specific Wednesday. He counted the passes silently, holding his corrections like water in his mouth, letting four go by. On the fifth, when a boy froze with the ball and the defender swarmed him, Blake blew the whistle and said only, "Too slow, you knew it."

The boy nodded, not looking at the sideline this time, and set up to run it again.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: On level ground without air resistance, the time of flight equals twice the initial vertical velocity divided by g, because rising and falling take equal times.
story:
Thomas had built the launcher himself, from a door hinge and a length of PVC pipe, and by eleven o'clock on the morning of the science fair it had launched two hundred and eight marbles across the gymnasium. The table cloth was still puckered where a judge had leaned on it. His display board said PROJECTILE MOTION: THE CURVE YOU CAN TRUST, which now struck him as an act of hubris he would pay for.

"Fourth judge in twenty minutes," said Thea, who had come over from her own table, where a spectroscopy project she described as "beautiful and doomed" was drawing no one. "The physics teacher judge. Ms. Ahmadi."

"I know who she is."

"She eviscerated a kid last year. verbally. There were witnesses."

"That kid used a bar graph for categorical data."

"So he deserved it. Do you deserve it?"

Thomas looked at his notebook, at the column of times he had measured with a stopwatch borrowed from the track coach, and at the column of times his equations had predicted. They did not match. The predicted times were almost exactly half the measured ones, every single trial, and he had been staring at that factor of two since seven in the morning, the way you stare at a word you've spelled so many times it stops looking like English.

Farah appeared at his elbow with a paper plate of fair-funded cookies. "Farah, tell him the thing about Ms. Ahmadi."

"Already told him."

"Tell him the other thing. The girl at the water filtration table got her poster rejected because she used the word utilize. Twice."

"I'm not going to survive this," Thomas said, and meant it in the specific, numerical way, and Farah put a cookie on his notebook like a small brown offering.

He went back to the math while they argued about whether a judge could legally be fought. He had a launch speed. He had an angle, thirty degrees, marked with a protractor taped to the hinge. From those he had split the velocity into a horizontal part and a vertical part, which was the whole trick his project was supposed to demonstrate, that the ball doesn't know it's on a curve, that it's two straight-line problems happening at once. The horizontal part carried the marble out at a steady rate, and the vertical part fought gravity and lost. His predicted time of flight came from dividing the vertical velocity by 9.8. Six trials later, his stopwatch kept insisting the marble stayed in the air nearly twice as long.

"You look like a man doing taxes," Thea said.

"I'm off by a factor of two."

"Half or double?"

"Predictions are half of reality."

He had written the launch angle on the board. He had written the speed. He had written his equation for time, v over g, and beside it the measured times, and between those two columns the factor of two sat there like a key he was holding while standing at a locked door.

Then the marble went up in his mind, not out, and he saw it. He had found the time to the top of the arc. That was what v over g gave him. And the top of the arc was only halfway through the flight, because rising and falling are mirror images of each other. The marble climbs until gravity spends all its vertical speed, and then it falls, and without air resistance the fall is the climb run backward. Equal times. The whole flight is twice the time to the top, so time of flight equals twice the vertical velocity divided by g.

"Both," Thomas said aloud.

"Both what?"

"Rising and falling take equal times. I only counted one of them." He grabbed a pen and wrote the doubling into the margin, and then, because his hand was shaking slightly, into the column of predictions, one by one, and the numbers lined up. Every trial. The stopwatch and the equation agreed to within a tenth of a second, and Thomas stood in the gymnasium of his high school with a hinge and a pipe and felt something open in his chest that he would not have been able to name without embarrassing himself.

Ms. Ahmadi arrived at his table at 11:52. She fired the launcher once, without asking, caught the marble on the first bounce, and read the board in silence. Then she read his notebook, which he had not intended, which showed the whole morning's failure.

"You found your error," she said.

"I found it, yeah. I got the time to the top and forgot the whole flight is twice that. Since rising and falling take equal times."

She nodded once. She wrote something on her clipboard. "Your board still says the predictions were low," she said. "The presentation disagrees with the notebook. The notebook is the better document." She put the marble down and moved on to the boreal-forest carbon table, where a boy in a lanyard was explaining permafrost to nobody.

Farah read the clipboard reflection over Thomas's shoulder, upside down. "Third place," she said. "The filtration girl got second. For utilizing things."

Thomas laughed, and started peeling the old graph off his board, which left a rectangle of brighter blue where the sun hadn't reached it, so that his display would show, for the rest of the afternoon, the exact shape of his mistake.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
Alice had the sheet music open on the stand before she even sat down, because that was how she had always begun: notes first, fingers second. The summer between high school and college had a strange looseness to it, a liminality she kept noticing in herself, as if she were standing in a doorway and had forgotten which room she was heading for. She had decided to spend part of it learning the violin, and Mr. Patel's summer class at the community center met in a music classroom with mismatched chairs and a poster of the orchestral families peeling at one corner.

The problem appeared in the second week, in the shape of a nine-year-old. Nikola, who was apparently some kind of prodigy of the afternoons, sat two stands down and played the whole first Suzuki book from memory, fingers landing without hesitation. Alice, who had spent four years in choir reading solfège fluently and could sight-sing almost anything put in front of her, was still fighting her third song. When Mr. Patel asked Nikola to play something from page twelve, Nikola played it, bright and clean. Then Mr. Patel set the open book in front of him and asked him to name the notes.

Nikola stared at the page like it was a plate of alphabet soup. "I don't know which ones those are," he said. "I know how it goes."

Alice looked from the page to Nikola's face and felt something tilt inside her. She had been congratulating herself on being the literate one, the one who could read, and here was a child who could speak the language but not write it. How did that even happen? She cornered Mr. Patel after class, polishing rosin off her strings.

"How can he play all that and not read a note?"

Mr. Patel shrugged, stacking chairs. "Ask him. He'll tell you faster than I will." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and Alice understood she was being handed the question rather than the answer.

So she asked Nikola the next afternoon, in the interval while Mr. Patel helped a student tune. Nikola was happy to explain, the way nine-year-olds are happy about their own expertise. "It's the Suzuki method," he said. "This man Suzuki, he was a violinist in Japan, and he taught kids to play by ear first, before reading music. Like how you learn to talk before you learn to read." He demonstrated by playing a phrase Alice had never heard, then repeating it with one note changed, watching her face to see if she caught it. She did. It was like watching someone bend a spoken sentence into a question.

She tried it that night in her bedroom, hunting a melody from the radio by ear, no paper on the stand. It was humiliating and thrilling at once. Her ears, it turned out, were slower than her eyes; she kept reaching for the visual shape of a phrase and finding nothing there, and having to listen instead, really listen, the way she had to actually look at a person to draw them. She had always been able to compartmentalize, to keep theory in one drawer and performance in another, and now the drawers were jammed open and mixing.

Her friend Larry, who had come over to borrow her physics notes, watched her saw through the same four bars eight times. "You're worse at this than calculus," he said, with his usual acerbic affection, and she laughed because it was true and because it didn't matter. What mattered, she was starting to think, was the question underneath it: whether the two ways of knowing could be stacked, ear under eye, instead of set against each other. Speaking before reading, then reading on top of it. Not either, but in what order, and why.

At the next class she asked Mr. Patel if she could try the book's early songs from memory, the way Nikola did, and still bring her note-reading along behind. He raised an eyebrow, which on him was a standing ovation. "Some people think the order matters a great deal," he said. "Some people think it matters not at all. Try it and tell me what you find." Nikola leaned over from his stand and offered, magnanimously, to play the tune once so she could steal it. She closed her book.

He played it. She played it back, wrong in three places, right in a way she couldn't yet name. He played it again, slower, grinning. She listened.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
story:
The loading dock smelled of cardboard and cold dust, and Xavier stood at a folding table with a thermometer in his hand, not sure yet whether he was allowed to make the call he was already making in his head. Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya had clipped a laminated sheet to the wall beside the refrigerator at seven that morning: refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius, 40 degrees Fahrenheit, to slow the growth of bacteria. Xavier had read it twice while the older volunteers were still arguing about where the pallet jack lived.

The milk had arrived at nine. A man in a church van had set four crates of it on the dock, on the sunny side, while he went back for a second load, and then the second load turned out to be a collapsed tower of dented tomatoes, and the milk had sat. Xavier only noticed when Precious nudged him and said, "Those have been out since the truck came. That's like an hour." She said it the way she said most things, flat and certain, as if the fact were already hers.

Xavier carried a carton to the thermometer and pressed the probe between two bottles. Nine degrees. He did it again on another crate, slower, wanting to be wrong. Eight and a half. He knew the numbers from the sheet, and he knew what his mother would say, his mother who kept the thermostat on the fridge at home so low the butter never softened. But the milk was the good stuff, whole milk, name brands, the kind the clients reached for first, and there were almost forty families on the list today.

"Ask him," Precious said, tipping her head toward the office, where Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya was on the phone with the county.

"He'll say no," Xavier said. "He has to say no. That's what the sheet is for."

"So ask him."

Harley came around the corner with a hand truck and stopped when he saw the crates. Harley had been volunteering since sophomore year, an acolyte of the whole operation, and he knew the rhythm of the place better than some of the staff. "Dock side's bad," he said. "Always has been. In August we lose something every week." He said it without drama, the way you'd report weather, and that steadied Xavier more than encouragement would have.

He went in anyway. Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya hung up and listened, and Xavier said it plainly: the milk had been on the dock in the sun for over an hour, it was reading eight and nine degrees, and the guidance on the wall said refrigerated food had to stay at or below 4 degrees Celsius, 40 Fahrenheit, to slow the growth of bacteria. Saying it out loud made it heavier than reading it had. He offered the half-formed solution he'd been carrying since the second reading: don't trash it automatically, call the donor pantry downtown, see if they had guidance for a partial excursion, maybe a use-don't-shelve policy like the one for dented cans.

"That's a lot of phone calls for milk," Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya said, but he was already reaching for the directory, which Xavier took as its own kind of answer.

While the call went on, Xavier moved the crates into the walk-in himself, sublimating the waiting into something physical, stacking and rotating so the oldest cartons faced out. Precious taped a sign to the dock door, SUN SIDE, CHECK BEFORE YOU SET ANYTHING DOWN. It wasn't official. It was marker on the back of an intake form. Harley read it and said, "He's going to leave that up for three years, you know," and Xavier believed him.

The call came back the way these things do, half and half. The downtown pantry couldn't guarantee the milk was safe to hand out, not knowing exactly how long it had been warm, but they offered to take it for their compost program, and Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya put forty families' worth of good cartons into the van himself, quietly, like a man returning something borrowed. On the way back he stopped at the wall sheet and stood in front of it for a moment. "Next donor run, you're on it," he said. "You'll ride with me. We'll talk to the church about coolers." Xavier nodded, then went to find the clipboard, because the tomatoes still needed sorting and Precious was already three crates ahead of him. He picked up a can, looked at the dent, held it to the light, and put it in the maybe pile.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something that a character on stage does not, which lets a short scene build tension quickly.
story:
The play was due in nine days, and William had written nothing but a title, "The Kitchen, August," which he had crossed out twice in his notebook. He had come to his grandmother's house because it was empty in the afternoons, his grandfather now in a chair by the window where he used to stand at the stove, and because the moment William wanted to write about had happened in that kitchen. His friends Aspen and Thalie arrived on the bus at four, carrying a bag of chips and a printed copy of the assignment sheet, which Mr. Walker had signed at the bottom with a note: ten minutes, one moment from your own life, staged for the class.

"Whose moment?" Thalie asked, dropping onto the couch. "Yours, right? It has to be yours."

"Mine," William said. "But it happened to all of us a little."

The moment was this: two Augusts ago, his grandfather had burned the sausages badly enough to set off the smoke alarm, and while the family stood coughing in the driveway, William had gone back in to get the old man's jacket and had found, folded inside it, a letter from a hospital. He had read three lines of it, then put it back, and said nothing to anyone for eleven days, until his mother found the letter herself and the house turned into a week of phone calls and weeping and his grandfather's diagnosis becoming a thing with a name. Eleven days in which everyone laughed at dinner while William watched his grandfather eat.

"Okay," Aspen said, when William had laid it out on the coffee table like evidence. "So the play is the dinner scene."

"If the audience knows about the letter first, the dinner is unbearable," Thalie said. "In a good way."

William had half-known this already, from a Tuesday when Mr. Walker had read a scene aloud from a photocopied packet and the whole class had leaned forward, and someone had said the word aloud, dramatic irony, and Mr. Walker had only nodded and turned the page, because the packet explained it: when the audience knows something a character on stage does not, a short scene builds tension fast. William had written the phrase in his notebook and underlined it, and now, in his grandmother's living room, he understood it as a tool rather than a term, something you could actually hold.

He tried the first version that evening. Aspen played the grandfather, standing at an imaginary stove, and Thalie played William's mother, and William played himself, sixteen and holding a plate. The scene was flat. Everyone said their lines and the room stayed cool. Then Thalie said, "Show us the letter first," and they rearranged it: the play opened with the boy alone, finding the folded page in the jacket, holding it into the light long enough for the audience to read the hospital's letterhead, then returning it to the pocket and going to sit down at the table. Only after that did the family enter, laughing, passing the sausages, asking the boy to say grace.

This time Aspen, mid-sentence as the grandfather, stopped and looked at the audience and said, "Pass the mustard," and the room went silent, because everyone watching knew what the boy at the table knew and the man asking for mustard did not. Thalie shivered theatrically. "That's it," she said. "That's the whole thing. Ten minutes of that."

They ran it again after his grandmother came home with groceries, and she stood in the doorway without taking off her coat, watching Aspen mime her husband's small joke about the neighbors' sectarian lawn signs, a joke he really made, and when the scene ended she said, "He still makes that one," and went into the kitchen, and the three of them sat without speaking until the water ran.

William wrote until midnight at the kitchen table, under the light where his grandfather had done the crossword. He was honest with himself in the margin of the page, where no one but he would look: he could not decide whether the eleven days of silence had been a kind of protection or a small attempt to expiate something, his cowardice maybe, or his wish not to be the one who broke the family's August. There were two ways of thinking and he could hold both at once, the way you can hold that a secret kept is kindness and also theft, and he did not try to resolve it in the script. He let the boy at the table simply pass the mustard.

The next morning he read the finished scene aloud to his grandfather, changing the diagnosis to something unnamed, changing the names, keeping the jacket and the letter and the dinner. His grandfather listened with his eyes on the window.

"Which one are you?" he asked at the end.

"The boy with the plate," William said.

His grandfather was quiet for a while, his hands folded on the armrest, hands that had fed a family for fifty years, bound to them all by blood and argument, by consanguinity and by choice. Then he said, "You can stage it in the kitchen if you want," and reached for his jacket, which was hanging on the back of the chair, and William watched him take from the inside pocket a folded piece of paper, fresh, and set it on the table between them without opening it.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults.
story:
Isabelle had worked at the garden centre for four Saturdays before Quinlan missed her first shift. The manager had written the schedule in green marker on the whiteboard behind the register, and Quinlan's name had simply not appeared in the flesh that day, nor the next, and by the third absence Isabelle was hauling the thirty-pound bags of potting soil alone, stacking them in the aisle while the smell of wet peat settled into her sleeves.

She found Quinlan on Monday at school, leaning against the lockers with her headphones around her neck. "You could text him," Isabelle said. "Just tell him you're sick."

"I'm not sick. I just didn't feel like going." Quinlan wound the headphone cord around one finger. "It's a plant store, Isabelle. Nobody dies if the marigolds don't get watered."

That evening Isabelle told her father about it while he chopped onions at the counter, and he shrugged the way adults shrug when they are deciding whether to say more. He worked in insurance, and he talked sometimes about how a single claim could underwrite a whole portfolio, how small risks compounded. "One missed Saturday is nothing," he said. "The question is what it becomes." He went back to the onions, and Isabelle carried the sense of unfinished conversation upstairs with her.

In the break room on Thursday she found Rogan, a senior who had worked at the garden centre for two years and could identify every seed packet by colour alone. He was eating a sandwich over a psychology textbook, and beside his elbow lay a photocopied page. "What's that?" she asked.

"Dunedin Study. New Zealand. They followed a thousand kids for decades." He turned the page toward her. "My sister's doing it in college. There's an analysis from 2011 about self-control. The kids with lower self-control ended up, as adults, with poorer health, less wealth, and criminal convictions, more often than the kids with more of it."

Isabelle read the line twice. "So Quinlan's doomed because she skips shifts?"

"I didn't say doomed. I said it's a study." Rogan took a bite of his sandwich. "My sister says the interesting part is it's not about one decision. It's about what the decisions are made of."

That Saturday, Quinlan showed up. She arrived twenty minutes late, smelling faintly of someone's bonfire, and she worked the register with her hair falling over the price codes until Ms. Ferreira, the woman who ran the herb greenhouse next door and came in for coffee refills every weekend, set down her cup and looked at her for a long moment without saying anything. Quinlan straightened afterward, but only for a while.

Isabelle rang up a woman buying three trays of basil and listened to Quinlan behind her, arguing with the manager about whether she could leave early. His voice was flat, not angry, the voice of a man subtracting something quietly. She thought of her father's portfolios, of Rogan's photocopy, and she understood that she had been carrying two different pictures of Quinlan and could not make them into one. In one picture, Quinlan was a girl who would figure it out, whose lateness was weather that would pass. In the other, Quinlan was already accumulating, each skipped shift a deposit into an account she could not see. Isabelle did not know which picture was truer, and she noticed that not knowing did not let her off; it only made her choice about herself sharper. She had been half proud of her own reliability, half contemptuous of it, as if showing up were a small and obedient thing. Now it seemed more like a wager: she was betting that the small things were the large things in disguise.

She had also, she had to admit, been a little intransigent about it, correcting Quinlan's schedule errors out loud in the break room where everyone could hear, which felt less like helping and more like performing. An ideologue about punctuality, Rogan had called her once, laughing, and she had laughed too, but the word had stuck to her afterward like a price sticker.

At closing, Quinlan asked her to wait and walk out together. The air outside had the green smell of the greenhouse rows cooling in the dark, and somewhere a sprinkler ticked against plastic. "You think I'm screwing up," Quinlan said. "Everyone thinks it. Ms. Ferreira looked at me like I was something she'd find wilted."

"I don't know what you are," Isabelle said. "I read this thing, about kids followed for decades. Lower self-control, and thirty years later their health and their money and their records were worse. It scared me, honestly. Not about you. About everything."

Quinlan was quiet past the first row of parked cars, her keys already in her hand. "Thirty years," she said. Then she unlocked the door and stood there holding it half open, looking back at Isabelle over the roof of the car.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Marxist historian Albert Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class.
story:
The war memorial stood at the edge of the park where the town kept its older griefs, a granite column ringed by names John had never read all the way through. He sat on the bottom step with his laptop balanced on his knees, the screen too bright in the October afternoon, and tried to make his outline behave. Ms. Hu had assigned a historiographical essay, which was not the same as a history essay, and the difference was the whole problem. He was supposed to write about how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, which meant writing about historians arguing rather than about revolutionaries starving.

He had coaxed himself here with the promise that a change of location would unclog him, and had then spent forty minutes producing one sentence. Cohen had tried to cajole him out of the assignment entirely that morning, leaning across the lab bench, saying he could just string the textbook's paragraphs together and call it analysis, everyone did. John had said maybe, and had hated how easily the maybe came.

Footsteps on the gravel path. Elliana dropped onto the step beside him, a museum brochure folded in her hand. "I thought you'd be here. Ms. Hu said you'd declared war on your own draft."

"I've reached a stalemate," John said. "I have three historians and no argument. One of them says the Revolution was basically a good idea that went wrong, one says it was doomed from the start, and one says it made the modern world, so, congratulations to it."

"Which one's the modern world one?" Elliana smoothed the brochure open on her knee. It was from the regional history museum, the one with the new permanent gallery she'd visited on the weekend. "Because I found something. Look." She tapped a caption beside a reproduction of a sans-culotte's petition, printed in a calm institutional font. "Read what it calls 1789."

John read it aloud. "A bourgeois revolution." The phrase sat there, ordinary as a date. "Whose interpretation is that? It's stated like a fact, like the caption's just telling you what happened."

"That's what got me," Elliana said. "I asked the woman at the desk and she just pointed at the gift shop. So I photographed it and came to find you, because you're the one who actually reads the footnotes."

He took out his phone and searched, half expecting the caption to be a museum invention, something softened for general audiences. Instead the trail led backward through citations to a French historian, Albert Soboul. John read the sentence twice under his breath. "Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class," he said slowly. "So the caption isn't neutral. Somebody chose Soboul."

"Somebody always chooses," Elliana said. She looked out at the column of names, the ones from the war his great-grandfather had survived and the ones from wars nobody in town remembered firsthand. "Is that bad? Choosing?"

John didn't answer right away, because the question had opened something in the outline that he hadn't known was there. He had been treating the historians like witnesses to the same event, disagreeing because they'd looked from different windows. But Soboul hadn't just looked from a different window. Soboul had a whole theory of history, classes rising and falling, and the Revolution fit into it like a stone in an arch. The other historians had their own arches. Maybe the essay wasn't about whose facts were right. Maybe it was about what each of them needed the Revolution to be.

"Here's the thing," he said, typing as he talked. "Soboul's explanation works, it's powerful, it explains why the Revolution happened when and how it did. But so does the other one, the one where it's a tragedy of good intentions. And so does the third. They can't all be the whole truth, but they're not exactly lying either."

"So what do you write?" Elliana pulled her jacket tighter. A wind had come up, scattering leaves against the memorial's base, where poppies from some ceremony weeks ago still lay browning.

"I don't know yet." He heard the malaise in his own voice and deleted nothing, because it was at least honest. "That's the part Ms. Hu keeps circling around without saying. Maybe I take Soboul seriously, take the others seriously, and say what I actually think, which is that Soboul's version explains the most and proves the least." He stopped typing. "Can I even say that? Proving the least and explaining the most?"

"You can if you say it like you mean it," Elliana said. "You're allowed to not resolve it. That's what my brother says about his thesis chapters, anyway, and he's the most pretentious person alive, so it must be true."

John laughed, and something in his chest loosened. He scrolled to the top of his outline and, instead of the three historians in a row like suspects, began arranging them as a conversation: one speaking, another objecting, Soboul answering last with the caption's confidence. He thought of the museum label again, how smoothly it had passed off a position as the past itself, and wrote in the margin, who is speaking? It was the first thing in two days he hadn't wanted to delete.

"Do you ever think this is an altruistic way to spend a Saturday?" Elliana asked, standing, gathering the brochure. "Sitting in the cold for dead French people."

"It's not for them," John said. "It's for whoever reads the next caption."

Elliana shoved the brochure into his hand. "Then get it right," she said, and walked off down the gravel path, her footsteps loud against all those carved and patient names.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
story:
The community art studio smelled of linseed oil and old coffee, and by the third Tuesday in October Charlotte had claimed the corner table near the window as her own. She spread her ten drawings across it like a hand of cards: ten views of the same abandoned bus stop on Delancey Road, drawn at different hours, in different weather, from different angles. The portfolio brief required ten artworks unified by a single theme, plus an artist's statement, and Charlotte had chosen thresholds, the idea that certain places hold you between two states of being. The bus stop was her hinge between school and home, between who she was at eight in the morning and who she was at six at night.

The problem arrived on a Tuesday when she counted eleven drawings.

She had stayed late on Sunday and drawn the stop in fog, the shelter's plastic panels gone soft and milky, a single figure inside like a specimen in a jar. It was, she thought, the best thing she had made in months. But the brief said ten. Ten meant ten, and Mr. Adeyemi, who ran the studio's Thursday critique nights, had a way of raising one eyebrow that could calcify a whole room's opinions into silence.

"You could drop the rain one," said Manreet, who worked at the next table and had taken to reading over Charlotte's shoulder without apology. "The fog one is better anyway."

"Then I'd have no rain. The whole point is the sequence. It's a day, sort of. It's a year, sort of." Charlotte squared the drawings against the table's edge. "It's the same place not being the same place."

Manreet made a noncommittal sound and went back to her collage, which was about, as far as Charlotte could tell, the colour of her grandmother's kitchen in Ludhiana and the colour of her aunt's kitchen in Brampton, and how the two kept arguing with each other across the page. Charlotte envied the certainty of it. Her own theme felt slippery whenever she tried to write the statement. She had drafted one that used the word liminality, which she had looked up after seeing it in a gallery label, and then deleted it, and then typed it again. It meant the state of being in between, and she liked it, but she wasn't sure she liked liking it. It felt like wearing someone else's coat.

She carried the fog drawing to the flat file where Mr. Adeyemi kept the studio's art books, looking for a distraction she could justify as research. Under a heavy monograph on Japanese prints she found what she wanted: a spread of small blue and grey images of a mountain, wave after wave of them, the mountain appearing behind boats, through fences, beyond rooftops, smaller than a thumbnail in some, enormous in others.

Manreet drifted over and read the caption aloud. "Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well."

Charlotte looked up. "Wait. Say the numbers again."

"Thirty-six in the title. Forty-six in the box. Ten extra." Manreet tapped the page. "It got popular, so he just kept going."

Charlotte sat down on the stool beside the flat file and did the arithmetic twice, as though the numbers might not hold. A famous series, named for a number, had outgrown its own name and nobody had corrected the name. The extra ten hadn't been hidden or apologized for. They were right there in the museum's spread, the storm beneath the mountain, the little blue peak behind a low fence. She wondered whether the title had become a kind of doorframe: the frame stayed the same size and the artist simply walked through it carrying more than it was built for.

"I have eleven," she said slowly. "The brief says ten."

"So?"

"So maybe the brief is a title, not a box." She turned the phrase over, testing it. It sounded clever, and cleverness made her suspicious, but she kept turning it anyway. Was she reasoning toward the truth or away from her own attachment to the fog drawing? She couldn't yet tell the difference, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that, at least inside her own head, where no eyebrow could reach her.

At Thursday critique she laid out all eleven and read her statement aloud, the liminality one, the version that described the bus stop as "a place that holds you between where you were and where you are going." She kept her voice steady on the last line: "The series is called Ten Views of the Delancey Stop and it contains eleven, because the fog came late and it belonged." She looked at Mr. Adeyemi, whose eyebrow began its climb, and then, surprisingly, came back down.

"Read us the bit about the mountain again," he said, and she did, the numbers, the dates, the ten added after the first ones sold, all of it, out loud, into the quiet room. He looked at the drawings a long time, the dawn ones and the noon ones and the fog one at the end like a held breath.

"Bring the rain one too, if you find a twelfth," he said at last, and turned to Magnus, who was presenting next.

Manreet caught Charlotte's eye across the table and mouthed, forty-six. Charlotte grinned, gathered her eleven drawings against her chest, and slid the fog one back on top, where the figure in the jar waited, patient, in the milk of the plastic glass.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
The day after the funeral, everyone gathered at Grandmother's house because nobody could decide what else to do with the casseroles. Thomas stood in the kitchen doorway holding a tray of cups he had been asked to fill and not fill yet, and watched his sister at the counter. She had laid out the recipe cards in a fan, the way Grandmother used to when she was deciding, and she was talking. Not narrating for anyone's benefit, not performing grief. Talking, quietly, to the empty chair: "I know, the nutmeg thing, I messed it up again." Thomas put the tray down and went outside.

He would say, later, that he was fine that day. He told Rosemary so on Monday, when she asked how the weekend had gone, and he said fine in the flat voice that usually ended conversations. But the truth, which he kept rearranging, was that he had not been fine, and that walking out of his grandmother's kitchen had been the least fine thing he had done in months. He was seventeen days from moving into his dorm, and some part of him had already put the whole summer on furlough, suspended until it could be dealt with at a safer distance.

His sister's talking to the cards bothered him more than the funeral had. At the funeral there had been a script, and Thomas liked scripts. He had read his part at the lectern without his voice doing anything embarrassing. But the kitchen had no script. It was just his sister choosing not to let go, and he had decided, on the porch, that someone in the family ought to say so. He spent the afternoon composing a scathing version of the speech, then a gentler one, then abandoning both when an uncle asked him to help carry folding chairs.

It was Rosemary who knocked that plan sideways. They were in the school library Tuesday, supposedly printing housing forms, and she was telling him about her mother, who kept her own mother's gardening gloves in the car and wore them every spring. "My dad used to think she should box them up," Rosemary said. "Then he read this thing." She pulled a thin book from her bag, a title stamped in sober letters on a worn cover: Continuing Bonds. "Came out in 1996. Klass, Silverman, and Nickman wrote it." She turned it over in her hands. "The whole argument is that keeping a connection with someone who's died is normal. Not a failure to move on. Normal."

Thomas took the book because refusing it would have required an explanation. He read it that night in bed with his door shut, and he kept catching himself arguing with it, and then catching the arguments falling apart. He had assumed grief was a door you walked through and closed. The book was full of people who had not closed it, parents and children and widows who kept talking, cooking, planting, and who were not stuck. Some of the case studies unsettled him. Some felt like his sister's kitchen with the names changed. He fell asleep with his thumb holding a page and woke with his heart palpitating, the book on the floor, his face stiff in a way he chose not to examine.

He went back to Grandmother's house on Thursday, alone, on the excuse of retrieving a box of his things. His sister was there again, of course, because she had never left, because she was making the lemon squares wrong on purpose to get the card to tell her so. Thomas stood in the doorway a second time, in nearly the same spot, and this time he came in. He set the book on the counter next to the fan of cards without a speech, without the version he had rehearsed, which now struck him as a stranger's words anyway.

"What's this," his sister said, but she wiped her hands and opened it.

"It says you're allowed," Thomas said. "That's all. It says it's normal." He hesitated, because honesty cost something here. "I thought it wasn't. I was going to tell you to stop." She looked at him over the top of the page, and he could not tell whether the look was forgiveness or just attention, and he decided he could survive not knowing. He pulled the nutmeg down from the shelf where it had always been and set it beside her elbow. "She kept it behind the flour," he said. "You've been using the wrong one."

His sister laughed, one wet syllable, and tapped the card with two fingers. "See," she said to the chair, "he does listen to you."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
Makena's birthday party had reached the stage where the cake was a memory and the remaining guests had sorted themselves by loyalty to the playlist, and Emile found Nicolas alone at the snack table, building what could only be described as a sandwich with structural ambitions. Nicolas was a gourmand of party food, impervious to shame on the subject, and he layered salami and potato chips with the solemnity of a man laying bricks.

"You're not listening to the song," Nicolas said, without turning around. "You have your feedback face on."

"I don't have a feedback face."

"You have a whole feedback vocabulary of faces. That one is the one you make before you tell someone their robot is slow."

The robot. Their robotics team had a competition in eleven days, and the drivetrain Nicolas had built was fast, elegant and, in Emile's opinion, drifting two degrees left on every full run. He'd watched it happen at four practices. He'd said nothing at four practices, and so had everyone else, because the code was Makena's, the arm was another teammate's, and mentioning the drift felt like pointing at the sun and complaining about the glare.

"You noticed it too," Emile said. It wasn't a question.

Nicolas finally turned, holding the sandwich like evidence. "Everyone noticed it. Makena noticed it. She noticed it and then she said, 'Nice run, everyone,' and started packing up."

"Why would she say that if she saw it?"

Nicolas shrugged and took a bite, and Emile watched him chew and thought about a page he'd photographed in his mother's office back in September, from a management book she'd left open on the printer. He'd read it twice on the bus. A researcher named Amy Edmondson had called it psychological safety in 1999, a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. At the time he'd thought it sounded like a phrase from a poster in a guidance counselor's office. Now he stood in Makena's kitchen with a paper plate going soft in his hand and suspected it was the most concrete thing he'd ever read, because their team did not have it, and the robot drifted left, and nobody had said a word for two weeks.

"Okay," Emile said. "Here's the thing. The drivetrain drifts left."

"I know."

"You know? You built it and you know?"

"I suspected it and then I told myself it was the floor in the lab being uneven." Nicolas said this with real dignity, crumbs on his shirt. "Floors are often uneven. That is a known fact about floors."

"So we've both been protecting each other from a two-degree problem for two weeks because nobody wanted to be the person who said the run wasn't clean." Emile set down his plate. "That's insane. We're not polite, we're just cowards with good posture."

Nicolas pointed the sandwich at him. "You're going to proselytize now. I can feel it. You get a concept in your teeth and you can't let go."

"I'm not proselytizing, I'm, okay, I'm a little proselytizing. But listen. Edmondson called it psychological safety, this thing where a team believes it's safe to take an interpersonal risk, like admitting a mistake. That's all it is. It's not being nice, it's not a feelings workshop. It's whether Makena thinks she can say 'my code might be the problem' without everyone going quiet like she's announced something contagious."

Nicolas considered this long enough to finish the sandwich. "So what's your plan? Walk up to the birthday girl at her party and tell her her code drifts?"

"No. Yes. Sort of." Emile had in fact been rehearsing a version of this all evening and every version had ended with Makena nodding politely and the problem surviving another week. "The problem is I do feedback like a trial. 'The drivetrain drifts left.' Verdict, delivered, exit. It's specific and it's cruel, or it's kind and so vague it's useless. 'Nice robot, it really has presence.'"

"It does have presence," Nicolas said. "The robot has more presence than most people I know."

Makena appeared in the kitchen doorway then, holding a stack of plates, and both of them straightened as if caught discussing her, which they were. "You two look like you're planning something," she said. "If it's the playlist, I've already been informed my taste is a crime."

Emile took a breath. He had two sentences, and he had promised himself he would keep the specific and the kind in the same sentence instead of letting one cancel the other out. "The drivetrain drifts left, about two degrees on a full run. I think it's brilliant engineering that needs one adjustment, and I didn't say anything at practice because I didn't want to be the guy who finds the problem. Which was worse, actually. Not saying it."

The kitchen went quiet enough that they could hear the party beyond the door, someone laughing at something in the other room. Makena set down the plates.

"Two degrees," she said.

"Every run. I timed it."

Makena looked at the ceiling, then at Nicolas. "And you knew?"

"I suspected the floor was uneven," Nicolas said. "I have since revised my position on the floor."

"Eleven days," Makena said, mostly to herself, and then she pulled out her phone and opened the calendar, and Emile understood that the team had just changed shape slightly, in a kitchen, over crumbs. "Tomorrow, the lab, nine a.m. Bring the timing data. And Emile, next time, say the thing at practice, not at my party."

"Understood," Emile said. "Happy birthday, by the way."

"There's cake left," she said, already typing. "The corner piece with all the frosting. You've earned the corner piece."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
story:
The Tuesday lab smelled of burnt coffee from the supply room and something faintly acidic from the sinks, and Elijah had claimed the station by the window because the light there made the numbers in his notebook look more decisive than they were. Mr. Mokoena had written the assignment on the board in his narrow, tilting hand: heat a measured mass of magnesium, predict the mass of magnesium oxide you should get, then weigh what you actually got. Elijah had read it twice and felt the small, visceral drop in his stomach that came whenever a question refused to stay on paper and insisted on becoming a real object on a real balance.

He had done the first part already, at home, the night before, which was unlike him. Four hundred and eighty milligrams of magnesium. He had converted that to grams, divided by the molar mass, and gotten a number he trusted. The trouble was the second step. The equation sat in his book, balanced and smug, and he had multiplied his grams by the ratio of the coefficients as if the little numbers were talking about grams, and the predicted product mass had come out absurdly, gloriously wrong. He had checked it three times over breakfast and the answer had not improved.

"You look like a man who has been personally insulted by a textbook," said Eleonore, setting her bag down at the neighboring station. She was already rolling up her sleeves, which was how she entered every lab, like a surgeon with somewhere else to be.

"I did the whole prediction last night," Elijah said. "It's wrong by a lot. Like, an embarrassing amount."

Krista drifted over, drawn by the word "embarrassing," which functioned among them as a dinner bell. "How much is a lot?"

"If my number were right, I'd get more product out than the magnesium and the oxygen combined. I'd have created matter." He slid the notebook across so they could see it, because sharing a bad number was easier than defending one alone.

Eleonore read it with her chin propped on her hand. Krista chewed the end of her pen, an old habit that Mr. Mokoena had given up trying to cure her of, and which he claimed explained the ennui of the pen caps that kept disappearing. For a while nobody said anything, and the crucibles ticked softly as the flames settled under them.

"Look at your units," Krista said finally, not unkindly. She tapped the line where he had multiplied grams by two thirds, the ratio from the balanced equation. "You put grams in. Grams came out. But did the equation ever say anything about grams?"

Elijah stared at the line. Something rearranged itself in his head, quietly, the way furniture moves in a dark room. "It says moles," he said slowly. "The coefficients give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses. I used it like a mass ratio." He said it out loud partly to hear whether it held together, and it did, the way a key holds when it turns. "So I take the grams, convert to moles first, and then the coefficients work."

"Congratulations," said Eleonore, deadpan. "You have discovered chemistry. It only took you until seventeen."

He redid it there at the bench, converting first, then applying the ratio, then converting back to grams for the final mass, and the new prediction sat in the notebook looking almost boringly reasonable. That was the thing about being right, he thought; it had none of the drama of being spectacularly wrong. He tried to hold both at once, the certainty of the arithmetic and the honest uncertainty underneath it, because the crucible had not been weighed yet and the real world had a habit of adding its own small argument. He did not want to dichotomize the evening into triumph or failure before the balance had spoken.

Mr. Mokoena came past on his slow circuit, hands clasped behind him, and looked at the corrected page for a long moment without touching it. "Better," he said, which from him was practically a parade. Then, to Krista, whose flame had gone the wrong color entirely: "And you, miss, are burning something that is not magnesium."

"That's very philosophical of it," Krista said, and turned the gas down.

When the crucible had cooled enough to touch, Elijah carried it to the balance with both hands, the way you carry something you have stopped making predictions about. Eleonore walked beside him out of pure, unembarrassed loyalty, and Krista trailed after, still smelling faintly of whatever she had burned. The reading came up on the display, and Elijah looked at it, and then at his notebook, and then back at the display, and let out a breath through his teeth.

"Close," he said. "It's close."

"How close?" Krista demanded, leaning over his shoulder.

"Close enough that I want to do it again before I believe it."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
story:
The travel agency smelled of old carpet and instant coffee, and Sebastian had been sitting under its flickering fluorescent panel for twenty minutes, waiting for his mother to finish arguing with Ms. Quinn about a refund. He had his geography binder open on his knees, and the photocopied population pyramid for Portugal lay flat across his math homework, a gray staircase of a graph with ages climbing one side and descending the other. Ms. Quinn leaned over the counter between phone calls and tapped it with a pen.

"School project?" she asked. "I used to hang those on the wall, back when the shop did actual research. Every country has a shape. Japan looks like an upside-down chandelier. Niger looks like a Christmas tree."

Sebastian explained the assignment, or tried to. He had to decide, from the shape alone, whether Portugal would need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years, and defend the decision in a paragraph. The pyramid's base was narrow, its middle bulged, and its top floors were, oddly, lopsided. The left side of each bar was shorter than the right. He had noticed it on the bus and had been staring at it since, sullen and restless, the way he got when a graph seemed to be keeping a secret from him.

"You look like my nephew when his phone dies," Ms. Quinn said. She slid a paper cup of coffee across the counter, though he was sixteen and she must have known it.

The door chimed and Elisha came in, jacket still zipped, having tracked Sebastian's location through a group chat. Elisha dropped into the chair beside him, snatched the pyramid, and held it at arm's length like a suspect. "Why's it crooked at the top? Did they print it wrong?"

"That's what I can't figure out." Sebastian turned the sheet sideways, then back. "The right side of every bar up here is fatter. Old women outnumber old men, like, across the whole top of the graph. It's not just Portugal, either. It's the same on the one for France in the textbook."

Elisha squinted, then delivered a verdict with total confidence. "It's because women live longer than men on average. My gran's got four sisters and they're all still going. Every funeral in her church is for some husband."

Sebastian checked it against the graph, age band by age band, the way his coach had taught him to check a defense before trusting it. The bars didn't start out uneven. Down at the bottom, at birth and through childhood, the two sides matched almost exactly, boys and girls in nearly equal numbers. The gap only opened as the ages climbed, widening decade by decade, until at the very top the women stood alone in a long thin shelf of gray. So it wasn't that more women were born. Something about surviving did it, and Elisha's gran and her church full of dead husbands suddenly looked like evidence.

"Okay," Sebastian said slowly, "but that doesn't actually answer the question." He pointed at the narrow base, the pinched young cohorts. "There are fewer kids coming up under a big crowd of old people. So it's nursing homes, obviously. Except." He hesitated, unwilling to prevaricate the way he might have in class, hedging until the bell saved him. "Except that fewer old men might mean fewer old people overall than I first thought, if the women are spread thin across more years. The graph doesn't tell me how long they stay in that top section. Two years, ten years, I can't tell."

"That's the most sullen cup of coffee I've ever poured," Ms. Quinn said, but she was smiling.

"Ms. Quinn said it used to be called an upside-down chandelier," Elisha offered. "A chandelier that's upside down. That's basically an oxymoron, right? Like a controlled explosion."

"It's not an oxymoron if it's just describing a shape," Sebastian said, and then stopped, because something had clicked sideways in his head. The two ideas, Elisha's grandmothers and his own narrow base, were not competing. They were both true, stacked on the same graph. His paragraph could hold both: more classrooms would not be needed, more care beds would, and the gender imbalance at the top meant that most of those beds, for most of those years, would hold women. It was not a clean answer. It was a careful one, with a margin of uncertainty he could actually name instead of hiding.

He borrowed Ms. Quinn's pen and wrote, in the margin of the pyramid, "not either/or, both at once, weighted." His mother was still at the desk, still not finished, and outside the window the streetlights were coming on over the wet pavement.

"Ready when you are," his mother called.

"In a minute," Sebastian said, and kept writing.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
The rink had shut down the public skate at six so the benches along the glass could fill with folding chairs, and by halftime of the pregame show Mr. Ndlovu had the big television mounted above the skate rental counter, its cord taped down in a way that suggested he had done this before. Chase sat between his grandfather and Sukhman, a plate of nachos balanced on his knees, while Tommy leaned over the back of his chair to steal chips with a shamelessness that had become, over the years, almost a form of affection.

"You know," the grandfather said, settling in the way he always did before a claim, "I remember the very first one of these. The first Super Bowl. I was there."

Tommy froze mid-theft. Sukhman, who had spent enough Sundays at Chase's house to know the terrain, went very still and studied the ice resurfacer parked behind the Zamboni garage as if it were a painting.

"Grandpa," Chase said, "you were there."

"Los Angeles. Packed house." His grandfather cracked a peanut with ceremonial calm. "Course, nobody called it the Super Bowl back then, not really. It was just the championship game. Packers and Chiefs. I saw it with my own eyes."

Chase did the math on his fingers under the nacho plate, quietly, the way you do when you suspect the answer will be awkward. He took out his phone and typed, low behind his wrist, and the screen told him what he already half knew: January 15, 1967, Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs, 35 to 10, Los Angeles. The whole fact sat there, complete and unhelpful, because his grandfather, in January of 1967, had been nine years old and living in Ohio, a fact Chase had heard at roughly forty Thanksgivings.

"Thirty-five to ten," his grandfather added, and Chase felt the nachos go heavy in his lap, because that part was right. The old man had the score, the teams, the city, the whole skeleton of it correct. It was only the "I was there" that had drifted, over fifty years of retellings, from his uncle's living room television into the stadium itself.

"It says here it was played on January fifteenth, 1967," Chase said carefully, tilting the screen. "In Los Angeles."

"There you go." His grandfather tapped the plate. "Coldest day of my life."

"It was in Los Angeles, Grandpa."

"Stadiums are drafty."

Sukhman made a small sound, a suppressed laugh escaping through his nose, and covered it by coughing into his sleeve. Tommy, who trusted the grandfather more than he trusted any phone, leaned down and squinted at the screen as though it might be lying about the date out of spite. Chase watched his grandfather's face and understood, with an affective certainty that no search result could allay, that this was not a matter of facts. Somewhere in the family there had been an uncle, long dead, whose living room had held that first game, and the living room had become the stadium the way a boy's memory of a story becomes the story itself. There was no jurisprudence for this, no court of appeal where you could file the record of what happened against the record of what was felt.

Mr. Ndlovu came around the counter with a tray of hot chocolate and set one in front of the grandfather without being asked. "You were at the first one?" he said, with genuine interest, because Mr. Ndlovu had grown up with football meaning an entirely different sport and was still collecting the American version like a second language.

"Front rows," the grandfather said. "Nearly froze."

"Drafty stadium," Chase said.

"Terrible," said his grandfather, and Mr. Ndlovu nodded gravely and said he had heard Los Angeles could be brutal in January, and Chase realized the two of them were now co-authors, and Sukhman had given up entirely and was laughing into his cocoa, and Tommy was saying "wait, so was it cold or not" in the tone of a boy trying to locate solid ground in a room where none was being offered.

Chase put the phone away. He could hold both things now, he found, without dropping either: the game had been played on January 15, 1967, in Los Angeles, where the Packers beat the Chiefs 35 to 10, and his grandfather had been there, in a living room in Ohio, nine years old, watching it through somebody else's uncle. Both of these were true, in the way that mattered, and only one of them was checkable. On the screen the anthem was starting, and his grandfather stood up out of respect, wobbling slightly, one hand on Chase's shoulder.

"Packed house," the old man said again, softer now, almost to himself. "Nobody thought it would become all this."

"That part's true," Chase said.

His grandfather squeezed his shoulder once, and did not sit down until the last note had faded, and even Tommy, out of some instinct he could not have explained, stood up too.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The community center rink smelled of burnt dust and cold rubber, and Autumn laced her skates on the bench nearest the door because from there she could see the whole sheet of ice, the scoreboard, and the hallway where her mother would appear at half past eight, waving regardless of the score. This was her second season with the league, the first in which she wore an A stitched on her jersey, and she had learned quickly that the letter mostly meant people asked her questions she did not know the answers to. Tonight the question was Emmanuel.

He took the hit in the second period, along the boards in the corner where the ice always rutted, and he went down in that particular way that made the whole bench stand without deciding to. He was up within seconds, skating to the bench on his own, and by the time the period ended he was laughing about it, ebullient in the way he got when he was frightened, telling Jeremiah that the defenseman hit like his little sister. Autumn watched him flex his left hand around the shaft of his stick, over and over, as though checking that it still belonged to him.

Between periods, the coach called her over. Emmanuel had begged him, loudly and in front of everyone, to be put back in for the final period, and the coach was a volunteer with a binder of drills and no medical training, a man who fixed furnaces during the day. "You took that certification course for the junior clinic, right?" he said. "The one they gave you the honorarium for. What does it say?"

Autumn had sat through the course in a carpeted room upstairs at this same community center, in August, mostly for the fifty dollars and the certificate with her name misspelled. She had expected to remember splints and ice packs. What she remembered instead, with sudden and inconvenient clarity, was a slide with a red border. "The guidelines say a player with a suspected concussion doesn't go back in the same day," she said. "Not even if they feel fine. That's the whole point of it. Feeling fine doesn't clear you."

Emmanuel heard. Of course he heard; he was three feet away pretending to retape his stick. "I feel fine," he said, and he said it with real anger, which was closer to the truth than the laughing had been. "Autumn, it's the last period. We're down by one. You want to just hand them the game?"

She had been ready for the argument about the game, and she had an answer that she believed: that the game was a thing made of nothing, a score on a borrowed scoreboard in a county league, and that Emmanuel was a thing made of everything, a person with a chemistry test on Monday and a sister who picked him up afterward. What she had not been ready for was the smaller argument underneath it, the one in his face. He was seventeen like her, and this was the last season before everything scattered, and he did not want to be the kind of person who lay down in a corner and came off the ice. She understood that wanting, because she had it too. Both things were true at once, and standing there with her mouth open she found she could not make one of them false.

"You could have a concussion and not know it," she said, more quietly. "That's why the rule isn't about how you feel. It's about the day. Same day, you sit. I didn't make it up."

"You're not a doctor," Emmanuel said.

"No. I'm the person who's supposed to say it anyway."

Mr. Carvalho, who ran the rink and was also the zamboni driver and also the man who had taught her junior clinic, came down from the warming room with a clipboard and a folding chair. He did not lecture anyone. He set the chair at the end of the bench and told Emmanuel to sit where he could be watched, and he asked him simple questions, what day it was, who they played last week, and he wrote the answers down while Emmanuel gave them, sullen now instead of ebullient, which Autumn decided was probably a good sign, though she kept the decision to herself.

The third period began without Emmanuel, and Autumn took his shift on the wing. They lost, two to one, on a goal that came with ninety seconds left, off a rebound she thought she should have had. In the hallway afterward, still in his pads, Emmanuel stood by the water fountain while his sister gathered his bag. "So what, I just convalesce at home like an old man?" he said. "For how long?"

"I don't know," Autumn said. "That part I don't know. Tomorrow you get checked, and then somebody who actually knows tells us. Tonight was the only part I was sure of."

He looked at her for a moment, then bumped her shoulder pad with the back of his glove, not gently and not unkindly. "Bring my stick to Monday's practice anyway," he said. "In case."

She said she would, and she zipped it into her own bag, right along the side where she could feel it when she carried everything out to the car.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: The phrase 'There ain't no such thing as a free lunch' was popularized by its use in Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress.
story:
Ethan had forty-one dollars in his back pocket and a photograph of the amp on his phone, saved from a listing two towns over. The amp was used, a little scuffed on one corner, and it cost ninety. He had done the math on the bus: four more weeks of skipping the coffee after school, and it was his. He was sitting in the coffee shop now anyway, because Kathleen worked Tuesdays and let him occupy the corner table for the price of nothing, drinking tap water from a glass she refilled without being asked.

He was halfway through a chemistry worksheet when Raven arrived, shaking rain off her jacket and talking before she had fully cleared the door. "The mall's doing a thing," she said, dropping into the chair opposite him. "You fill out a survey, ten minutes, and they give you a free gift. Kathleen says it's a mug. A fifteen-dollar mug, supposedly."

"Free mug," Ethan said.

"That's what the sign says." Raven peeled off her wet socks of words and got to the point, which was her way; she could be bellicose in an argument about almost anything, but she was honest about it afterward. "My brother says there ain't no such thing as a free lunch. He says Heinlein popularized that, in The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, 1966. He read it for a class and now he quotes it at dinner like he invented it."

"Who's Heinlein?"

"A writer. Science fiction. Apparently the book's about a lunar colony." She stole his worksheet and looked at it upside down. "Anyway, ten minutes of survey for a mug. That's not free, that's a wage."

Kathleen came over with a cloth and wiped the table although it was clean, which meant she wanted to talk. "It's not a wage," she said. "A wage is money. It's more like a trade. You give them your opinions and they give you a mug, and then they sell your opinions to somebody." She straightened the sugar caddy. "My manager calls the survey an enfranchisement, actually. The coupon inside it enfranchises you to one free drink, any size. She learned that word at a conference and uses it constantly."

Ethan looked at his worksheet and did not see it. In his head he was dividing things up. Ten minutes of survey, plus the bus to the mall, plus a free drink he would not otherwise buy. Against that: ten minutes of homework, or ten minutes of nothing, which he also valued, though he had never tried to say how much. His father had a way of talking about this at dinner, mostly about jobs he hadn't taken, roads he hadn't driven. Ethan had always thought of it as an old man's arithmetic, a counting of ghosts. But here it was in a coffee shop, in the small denomination of a mug.

The bell over the door rang, and Mr. Virtanen came in from the rain, retired, from three doors down, carrying a laptop under his arm like a plate of food he was tired of holding. He ordered a dark roast and, on his way past, set the laptop on their table. "You're the one who fixed the Hendersons' printer," he said to Ethan. It wasn't a question. "This thing won't connect to anything. If you can look at it, I'll insist on giving you something for your trouble. A small honorarium. My father was a pastor and that was the word they used when they paid him a little for a lot."

"I can look tonight," Ethan said. "It's probably the network settings."

"It's probably the network settings," Mr. Virtanen agreed, and left the laptop and went to his stool by the window with his coffee.

Raven leaned across the table. "So tonight you fix his computer, and you get paid, and that's the amp sooner. Or you do the survey and get the mug. Or you do your chemistry and get into a decent college, theoretically, in two years." She counted the options on her fingers, and he noticed she included doing nothing as one of them, which he found strangely generous. "You can't do all three at once."

"That's what my dad says. He calls it the next best alternative. You give up the next best thing, whatever it was."

"Your dad and my brother should start a club." Raven took her phone out, then put it face down again, an unusual act of restraint. "The thing I don't get is how you know which one was best. You only find out afterward, or you never find out."

Kathleen refilled his water, though he had barely drunk any. "My manager took the survey herself," she said. "She got the mug. It has a chip in the handle and she keeps pens in it."

Ethan closed the chemistry workbook. Mr. Virtanen's laptop sat between them, closed and a little damp at one corner, and outside the window the rain had thinned to something more like weather than like argument. He put his hand on the lid of the laptop. "Tonight," he said. "After that, I'll figure out the rest."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
Clara had the pre-registration form open on the family computer, third tab from the left, and she had been looking at the empty birthdate field for four minutes when Jannat leaned over her shoulder and said, "It's not a trick question."

"It's a decision," Clara said. "I'm deciding whether I'm the kind of person who does this."

"You're the kind of person who's sixteen," Jannat said. "In my state you can pre-register now and it just, like, activates later. It's the least romantic paperwork in the world."

Kole had a different view, which he had delivered that afternoon in the school parking lot with the confidence of someone who had recently discovered spreadsheets. Voting, he said, was a throughput problem. Millions of ballots in, one result out, and any single ballot made no measurable difference to the output. He hadn't meant it cruelly. He meant it the way he meant everything, as a system with inputs and losses. Clara had told him that was a way of describing a person as noise, and he had considered that seriously, which was the annoying thing about Kole, and then the bus had come.

At the kitchen table her grandfather was doing the crossword in pencil, as always, in case he needed to take an answer back. He was a taciturn man who communicated mostly through the pencil, tapping it when he disapproved of something on the television. Clara called across the room to him anyway, because he was the only adult in the house and because she wanted someone to disagree with Kole.

"Does voting actually matter?" she asked. "Like, in the arithmetic sense."

He didn't look up. "When I was your age, eighteen-year-olds couldn't vote at all," he said. "Then they were drafting eighteen-year-olds for Vietnam, and people started saying old enough to fight, old enough to vote. That's where it came from."

"That's it? That's the whole origin story?"

"That's the whole origin story," he said, and filled in a word, nine letters, and Clara went back to the computer feeling like she'd been handed something and wasn't sure what it was.

She searched the slogan and found old footage, grainy film of kids her brother's age holding signs with those words on them, old enough to fight, old enough to vote. She sat with her chin on her hand and watched a boy who could not vote be eligible for a draft, and she understood, in a preliminary way, that her boredom and his stakes were the same form filled out at different times. Kole's throughput argument assumed the input was worthless. The kids in the footage had argued, with their bodies, that the input was the whole point. Clara did not yet know how to hold both of those ideas at once, and she noticed that not knowing was uncomfortable in a way that felt productive, like a muscle she didn't have yet.

Jannat, meanwhile, had turned eighteen in March, and her laptop had died in April, which was how she came to be sitting at Clara's family computer on a Tuesday evening with the actual ballot on the screen, an actual general election, midterms, school board and a judge and two statewide questions. "Don't look," she said, and then, after a second, "Actually, look. I don't care."

Clara looked. The school board race had four names. Jannat went down the ballot clicking, and Clara watched her hesitate at the judge, hover, choose, and Jannat said, "I have no idea who that woman is. I'm voting for her because her bar association rating was good and because my mom said the other guy is a creep. That's the entire reasoning. Is that horrifying?"

"I think that's just what it is," Clara said. "Kole would say the system has bad throughput."

"Kole can compress my—" Jannat stopped herself, out of respect for the grandfather, and clicked Submit, and the screen told her, in the flat typography of the secretary of state's website, that her ballot had been recorded. Nothing happened. No sound, no change in the room, the grandfather still penciling his crossword, the kettle still not yet whistling. Jannat sat back and looked at the screen as though it owed her more.

"That's it?" Clara asked.

"That's it," Jannat said. "No parade. I've been eighteen for seven months and that was the entire ceremony." She paused. "It was still the most government I've ever personally touched."

Clara finished her pre-registration that night. She typed her birthdate into the field, which felt momentarily like an accusation, since the field clearly belonged to somebody older, and the website told her she'd be added to the rolls automatically when she turned eighteen, and she closed the tab and felt, honestly, nothing much. Two years is a long time to pre-commit to a position. People calcify around opinions they formed young; she'd read that somewhere, probably on Kole's phone, forwarded without comment. She did not want to calcify. She wanted to keep the question open, the way the ballot question was open, and the only way she could think of to do that was to keep showing up to it.
