She showed up to it imperfectly for two years. She argued with Kole, and once with a woman canvassing outside the grocery store, and she read one book about the war and half of another. Some of her certainty wore off. Some of Kole's wore off too, though he'd deny it. When the presidential year came, she found she still couldn't refute the arithmetic. One vote among millions did not decide anything. But the kids in the footage hadn't been making an arithmetic argument, and she had decided, gradually and without a single dramatic moment, that the arithmetic was the wrong ledger entirely.

On a Tuesday in November, at eighteen years and two months, Clara sat down at the family computer, the same chair, the third-generation version of the same website. The grandfather was at the kitchen table with his crossword, older, still in pencil. She entered her name and her birthdate and the ballot came up, longer than Jannat's had been, and she went down it slowly, and at the judge she stopped, because she had heard something about one of them that she hadn't checked.

"Pencil's on the table if you need to take something back," her grandfather said, not looking up.

"Votes don't work like that," Clara said.

"No," he said. "That's why we fought about it."

She clicked Submit, and the screen told her, in that same flat typography, that her ballot had been recorded, and she sat there while the kettle began, somewhere behind her, to warm up.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister.
story:
The essay was due at midnight, and by four o'clock Emma had written nothing but a title she already hated. She spread her laptop, two highlighters and a printed article across the corner table at the coffee shop, next to the window where the afternoon light came in flat and grey. Usman arrived first, shaking rain off his jacket, and Jimmy came ten minutes later, still voluble from a debate team meeting that had apparently ended without a winner.

"Perfect," Jimmy said, dropping into the chair across from her. "I need someone to settle this. Usman thinks a politician should be allowed to own a TV network if the voters know about it. I think it's insane."

"It's not insane, it's a question of disclosure," Usman said. "If everyone knows who owns what, the audience can adjust."

"Adjust," Jimmy repeated, as if the word had personally offended him.

Emma had planned to write about campaign finance, which she now suspected was the most boring subject available to an eighteen-year-old. She turned her laptop toward them. "What's the actual case you're fighting about?"

Usman pulled out his phone. "Berlusconi," he said, scrolling. "He kept control of Mediaset while he was prime minister. Mediaset owned three of Italy's main national TV channels."

"Three," Jimmy said. "While running the country."

"That's not the whole picture," Usman said, and Emma watched him scroll faster, which she had learned meant the picture was worse than he wanted to admit. Jimmy ordered an espresso at the counter and came back still talking, arguing that a prime minister with three national channels wasn't a politician, he was a weather system; everything bent around him whether or not he intended it.

Emma had opened a second browser tab before he sat down. She read while they went back and forth, and the reading complicated both of them. On Usman's side, the channels kept broadcasting, kept running entertainment and news, and audiences in a democracy were not children; they could hold two ideas at once, could watch a network and remember whose it was. That was Jimmy's side, or close to it, except Jimmy was being louder about it than the evidence required. She found an interview with an Italian journalist who said viewers had known exactly who owned the channels and watched anyway, which bothered Emma more than ignorance would have.

She had been raised on a kind of household rationalism, her mother's version of it, which held that every problem had a clean answer if you laid out the facts in rows. Facts in rows were on her screen now and they were not converging. Disclosure, which Usman trusted, was necessary and insufficient; the knowing audience was also an audience that had, for years, kept watching. At some point, she thought, a citizen's skepticism could atrophy from disuse, not because people stopped caring but because caring took energy and the channels were simply there, in every room, every evening, easier than doubt.

At five forty her phone buzzed. A message from Ms. Das, her politics teacher, who had apparently already seen the essay outline Emma submitted as a formality: "Campaign finance? You can do better. If you're near the shop on Wharf Street, I left a copy of something behind the counter last week, a special issue on media ownership. Ask for the folder. It's yours if you want it. Deadline stands."

Emma showed the message to Usman. He read it and shrugged. "She always does this. Makes you think it was your idea."

"That's what a good teacher does," Jimmy said.

She went to the counter and asked. The cashier produced a manila folder, soft at the corners, with a sticky note in Ms. Das's handwriting that said only, Emma, maybe. Inside was the special issue and, stapled to the back page, a photocopy of a two-page spread about Mediaset with a timeline along the bottom. Emma read the timeline standing up, elbow against the condiment station, while the espresso machine hissed through two cycles behind her. The timeline did not editorialize. It listed the channels, listed the years, listed the offices held, and let the rows sit there, adjacent, refusing to be a single sentence.

She carried the folder back to the table. Usman and Jimmy had moved on to arguing about whether debate club counted as a real sport, and she let them have it for a minute while she reread the photocopy. Then she closed the laptop's other tabs, the campaign finance ones, and opened a blank document. She typed the first line of the essay, deleted it, typed it again: If we agree that voters deserve to know who is speaking, we still have to decide what knowing is worth.

"It's six," Jimmy said, checking the time. "You've got six hours."

"I know," Emma said. She looked at the timeline again, at the prime minister's name and the three channels printed side by side, and thought that she would probably end the essay without a conclusion, because she did not have one yet that she believed. She pulled the keyboard toward her and started typing, and Usman, without being asked, slid his coffee out of the way of her elbow.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
story:
The print of The Broken Column had been taped to the art room easel since Monday, and by Wednesday Stella had stopped seeing it, which she suspected was the whole problem. Ms. Sow had assigned each of them a painting to critique using formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism, no "it made me feel sad" allowed. Stella had written "it made me feel sad" three separate times already and crossed it out three times, each deletion a small funeral.

"Why is there a Greek column inside a person?" she asked the room at large, because saying it aloud made it sound even stranger, which felt like progress. Maram, who was stretched across two stools doing her philosophy reading, looked up from a chapter titled, with terrible timing, utilitarianism. "Why is anything inside anyone? Blood. Bones. Two hundred thousand years of evolutionary compromise."

"That's not an answer, that's a mood," Stella said. Kaitlin, at the sink rinsing brushes she hadn't used, drifted over the way she always did when a conversation smelled like gossip, even academic gossip.

"It's an Ionic column," Kaitlin said, pointing with a wet brush. "The scroll-y kind. You can tell by the capitals, they look like rams' horns." She said this with the serene authority of someone who had read exactly one paragraph about architecture, possibly on a bus.

Stella leaned in. The figure in the painting stood against a cracked, russet landscape, and where her torso should have been seamless there was an opening, and through it her spine showed, painted as a cracked Ionic column, white and ridged, broken roughly in the middle. The rest of her body Stella could account for: the nails, the tears, the strap that held her together. The column was the part that refused to become inventory.

"Okay, but it's not decorative," Stella said slowly, talking mostly to the painting now. "It's load-bearing. It's her spine. It's structure disguised as ornament." She was reaching for something and could feel it slipping around the way a fish slips around your hands in shallow water.

"Careful," Maram said, lowering her book. "You're about to have a thought. I can see it in your face. It looks like heartburn."

"Formally, though." Stella grabbed her sketchbook and started drawing boxes, which was what she did when thinking got slippery. "The colour palette is mostly warm and dry, ochres and that suffocating green, and the column is the palest thing in the whole picture. Compositionally it's dead centre, vertical, the one stable line in a landscape that's literally splitting. So the symbolism has to come out of those choices, right? She paints herself as a building that failed."

"Or as a building that's still standing," Kaitlin said, and then ruined it by adding, "either way I'd get extra points for mentioning the nails, if I were you. Ms. Sow loves the nails."

Stella wrote half a sentence about the nails, stopped, and crossed it out. The nails were the easy part, the horror-movie part, the part any of them would notice on a bus. The column was harder because it did two jobs at once. It was a classical reference, all that Greek dignity and proportion, and it was broken, and it was also literally the thing holding her upright. Stella thought about her own habit of describing injuries as jokes, the way she'd told everyone her knee surgery was "a fun little refurbishment" while learning to recuperate on the couch for six weeks, rehearsing cheerfulness the way other people rehearse grief.

"So here's my position," she said, standing up, which was her move when she'd committed. "The painting isn't just showing pain. It's showing that the thing keeping her upright and the thing that broke are the same object. That's why it's an architectural element and not, like, a bone. Bones are private. Columns are public. She's putting her interior on the outside, which is also what the opening in her torso is doing, formally."

"I understood about forty percent of that," Maram said, "but the forty percent was pretty good."

"She's using formal analysis," Kaitlin announced to the room, delighted, as if reporting a rare bird. "She's got the disease. Ms. Sow said it's contagious this time of year."

"I'm still not sure," Stella admitted, and found, to her surprise, that admitting it made the position feel sturdier, not weaker. "Whether the column reads as her being ruined or her enduring depends on whether you think a broken column is still a column. I can argue both. Ms. Sow is going to hate that."

Ms. Sow collected the critiques on Friday, reading them at her desk while the class ostensibly cleaned. When she reached Stella's paper she read it twice, which Kaitlin monitored from across the room with the intensity of a nature documentarian. Then Ms. Sow looked up and said, "Stella, this is the strongest thing you've written all year. This is the piece you should be proud of." She paused, pen hovering. "You did realize, I assume, that I put this print up six weeks ago for the perspective unit, and you're meant to be critiquing your own still life, which was due Tuesday."

Stella looked at the easel, at the painting that had swallowed her whole week, at the column standing bravely in the ruin of her grade, and picked up her pencil.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time.
story:
Ava had agreed to write Evan a birthday melody, sixteen bars with chord changes, because he had asked her in front of people and she had not thought fast enough. That was Tuesday. The party was Saturday, and he wanted to play it on his grandfather's keyboard in front of everyone, which meant she needed actual notation, not the humming and hoping she usually did.

She set up at the kitchen table after dinner, while her mother recuperated on the couch with a book she was pretending to read. Staff paper, pencil, the keyboard app on her phone. She had decided on a simple plan, four chords that moved in a pattern she liked, one chord per bar, a melody floating over the top. The cerebral part, she told herself, was choosing the chords; the rest was just arithmetic.

The arithmetic was the problem. By Thursday night she had eight bars she liked, and bar nine kept coming out wrong. She wrote a melody that felt right when she played it, but when she counted the notes against the bar, she came up short. One beat, gone. She stared at the row of quarter notes and the long half note at the end and counted again, tapping her pencil. Two, then one, then nothing where the fourth beat should have been.

She texted Drew, who was in her music class and had opinions about everything. "Is notation allowed to just lie," she typed. "Like can a bar feel full and still be empty."

"Bar nine again?" Drew wrote back. "Send a photo."

She sent a photo. There was a pause long enough for Drew to have made a sandwich. Then: "Dude. Dot it."

"Dot what."

"Your half note. Put a dot after it. My cousin drove me insane with this all summer. A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time. You're one beat short. Do the math."

Ava looked at the half note, at the empty space after it, at her phone. She penciled a small dot beside the note head and counted. Two, and then the extra beat arriving out of nowhere, filling the bar exactly. She played it through. The melody sat down into the chord like it had been waiting for a chair.

"Why didn't anyone tell me this before," she wrote.

"You dropped music in grade nine to take fencing," Drew said. "There was a whole semester of dots you missed. Also I think you have to come to terms with the fact that notation was invented by people who hated you personally."

Friday she finished the remaining bars, some of them good, a few of them what she privately called filler with a melody line over it. The chords carried more of the last section than she wanted, but there was a kind of honesty in that, she decided, or at least a kind of deadline. She inked the final copy after midnight and left it on the keyboard bench.

Saturday afternoon, Mr. Jean-Louis, the retired teacher from next door who had somehow appointed himself the party's audio engineer, arrived with a metronome and a folding table. He set the sheet music on the stand with ceremony, and Evan sat down, cracking his knuckles like a man about to perform surgery.

"Composed by Ava," he announced to the yard. "Sixteen bars. I counted."

"You counted," Ava said.

"Twice."

He began to play. The melody came out slower than she had imagined it, and heavier, and by bar nine she had stopped hearing the notes and started hearing her own heartbeat, because he was approaching the dotted half note, her dot, her discovered beat, the small pencil mark that had fixed everything. He reached it. He held it. One, two, three. The bar filled perfectly and the chord shifted under it exactly as written, and Ava leaned back against the fence with the modest satisfaction of a person whose arithmetic had survived contact with an audience.

Then he kept going, and in bar fourteen he played a note she had never written, then another, and the melody wandered off the page entirely, improvising over her chords with an ease she would not achieve in ten years of Saturday afternoons.

"That bar fourteen," she said afterward, tapping the sheet music. "That's not what's written."

Evan looked at the page, then at her, and shrugged. "It sounded better."

"Then why did I spend a week counting beats?"

"Because," he said, gesturing at the yard full of people who were applauding him, "now I look like I can read music."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976, keeping nested squares constant while changing only the colours.
story:
The deadline for the portfolio was four weeks away, and Alyssa had eleven paintings she hated and one she could tolerate, which was, by her arithmetic, nine short of a theme. She had spread them across Mr. Hu's classroom floor after last bell, hoping the sight of them together would suggest something, the way a detective pins photographs to a corkboard. Kaelan stood over them with his backpack still on, chewing the stem of his glasses.

"They look like a group project where nobody talked to each other," he said. "That one's a lake. That one's, what, a hand?"

"It's a hand."

"It's a hand doing something to a door, possibly against its will."

Julius came in from the hall with two vending machine cookies and lowered himself into Mr. Hu's desk chair, which was against the rules, and spun once, slowly, for gravity. He looked at the floor for a long time. He was the only one of them who had actually gone to the Albers retrospective at the museum in the spring, alone, on a bus, which they had all made fun of and all privately envied.

"You know what he did," Julius said. "Albers. Over a thousand works in the Homage to the Square series, from 1950 until 1976. And it's the same nested squares every time. He kept the composition constant and changed only the colours."

"A thousand," Kaelan said. "Of squares."

"Over a thousand."

Alyssa crouched and picked up the one painting she tolerated, a rectangle of three windows at dusk, and something turned over in her, half excitement and half dread. She had been treating the portfolio as ten separate inventions, ten proofs of range, and the assignment sheet on Mr. Hu's desk had never actually asked for that. It asked for a theme. She had been exhausted by the wrong problem.

"So I keep the composition," she said slowly, "and change one thing."

"Could be colour," Julius said, mouth full of cookie. "Could be something else. Could be your windows, whatever's in them. Same three windows, ten times, and each time the light is different."

"Or each time something's been moved out of the room," Kaelan said. "Like the rooms are being emptied. Like somebody's leaving and you only see it sideways."

They argued about it for twenty minutes, and Mr. Hu, who had been pretending to organize a supply cabinet this whole time so as not to interrupt, finally said that the building closed at six and that the floor was not a gallery. On the bus home Alyssa wrote in her sketchbook: same windows, same proportions, only what's inside changes. Then she crossed out only and wrote one thing, because Julius had said the colours were the only variable, and she was already cheating, a little, and knew it. She felt the cheat clearly and kept it anyway. The rooms would empty, and the light would change too, because a room with a bed and a room without one do not hold dusk the same way. She would find out from the paintings whether that was two variables or one.

The first week she recuperated the paintings she already had, cutting down the lake, the hostile hand, the others, salvaging stretcher bars and gessoing over everything except the tolerated windows. It felt like demolition and it felt like harvest, and she surprised herself by laughing out loud at the sink when the hand reappeared, ghost-pale, through the third coat of primer, refusing to be erased. She let it stay. A hand on a windowsill, holding nothing, in a room where the bed is gone. She wrote in the margin of the artist's statement draft: even the paintings don't leave cleanly. Then she crossed that out too, because it was the kind of line a disaffected person puts in a statement, and she wasn't disaffected, she was just tired, which was different, and which the statement didn't need to confess.

On Friday she brought the first three finished pieces to Mr. Hu's room and laid them in a row, and Kaelan and Julius came, and a girl from third period who never talked to anyone stood at the edge of the group for a while and then said, quietly, "They get emptier," and Alyssa said, "Yeah," and turned the third one around so the light from the window fell across it the way it was painted to.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: The margin of error measures only random sampling error; it does not cover errors from badly worded questions, people refusing to answer, or poorly conducted interviews.
story:
Blake found the poll taped to the whiteboard before he even set down his bag: Quincy's handwriting, a bar chart, the headline "Seventy-Two Percent of Seniors Want the Bell Schedule Changed." Below it, in smaller letters, "+/- 5% margin of error." The student newspaper office smelled like toner and the cold pizza nobody had thrown out after Thursday's layout night, and Quincy was standing by the printer with the confidence of someone who had already won the argument.

"Two hundred responses," Quincy said, tapping the chart. "I did it right, Blake. Real math."

Blake pulled the survey sheet out from under a stack of layout proofs and read the question aloud. "'Given that studies show starting school later improves grades and mental health, do you support changing the bell schedule?' He looked up. "You gave them the answer in the sentence."

"It's persuasive framing," Quincy said. "Every real poll does it."

Londyn came in with two coffees and set one at Blake's elbow without being asked, because she had noticed him skipping breakfast all week. She read the question over his shoulder, chewed her lip, and said the thing Blake had been circling. "My mom does surveys for the county. She says half her job is fixing what the question did before anyone even answered it."

Blake sat down at the sticky laptop and opened his notes from the stats unit Ms. Suzuki had taught in journalism last spring. She had made them memorize it for the quiz, then never mentioned it again, which had seemed like cruelty at the time. He found the line and read it slowly, twice. The margin of error measured only random sampling error. It did not cover errors from badly worded questions, people refusing to answer, or poorly conducted interviews. He had written it down without understanding that it was a warning, and now the warning had a face, and the face was Quincy's bar chart claiming the senior class.

"Here's the problem," Blake said, and he kept his voice even, because Quincy had stayed up until two in the morning collecting those two hundred responses and Blake had seen the timestamp on the shared doc. "Your five percent only covers the randomness of who you happened to sample. It's the only thing it covers. The question steered people. And look at your respondent list, it's almost all seniors who follow the paper's account. The people who ignored the poll aren't in your five percent anywhere."

"So we shrink the headline," Quincy said. "Seventy-two becomes a range."

"It's not a range problem." Blake titrated his words carefully, aware that too much certainty from him would just make Quincy defensive. "The number could be anywhere. The math can't tell you where, because the math only ever promised to measure one kind of error, and it wasn't the kind you made."

Quincy sat down on the desk edge, deflating in stages. "I interviewed like forty people at lunch, too. Some of them I basically read the question out loud with feeling."

"That's the interviews," Londyn said gently. "Those count too."

For a while nobody spoke, and the radiator clanked its melancholic winter rhythm, the same sound it had made all through exam week, a kind of leitmotif for the paper's worst months. Blake watched Quincy's face and thought about how badly he wanted to be right himself, how satisfying it would be to replace Quincy's certainty with his own, and how that would be the same mistake wearing better clothes. The honest position was smaller: the poll told them something, but not what the headline claimed, and exactly how much it told them was the part nobody could compute.

"Okay," Blake said. "What if we run it differently. 'How Seniors Responded to a Question About the Bell Schedule,' and then a sidebar where we show the exact wording, admit it was loaded, and explain what the margin of error does and doesn't cover. Let readers see the machinery."

Quincy was quiet, rubbing a coffee ring on the desk with his thumb. "That's embarrassing."

"It's more embarrassing to get fact-checked by Ms. Suzuki in front of the class," Londyn said, and Quincy almost laughed, a short exhale that broke the tension enough to move in.

They rewrote the headline together, Quincy typing, Blake dictating the sidebar language, Londyn untangling the chart from the whiteboard without tearing it. At the door, Quincy paused with his coat half on. "Next survey, you write the questions first. Before I touch anything."

"Deal," Blake said, and held up the loaded original, the offending sentence still visible, and pinned it to the corkboard next to the revised page.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, a landlord may collect a rent deposit of no more than one month's rent, or one rent period if rent is paid more often, but may not charge a damage deposit.
story:
Jasmine had spread both leases across the little table in the bank's customer alcove, the way other people spread maps. One was for a basement room near campus with rent of nine hundred a month, all utilities included except internet. The other was a bright seventh-floor studio at eleven hundred, heat and water included but hydro separate, and hydro, according to the listings she had been reading all week, could run anywhere from forty dollars in a mild month to double that when the air conditioning ran. She had a notebook, a calculator she kept setting down and picking up again, and a bus to catch in forty minutes.

Lili arrived first, sliding into the chair across from her with a paper cup of something that smelled like burnt caramel. "Tell me you're not doing math at a bank."

"I'm doing math at a bank," Jasmine said. "Lionel's meeting me. He already did this last year, before he found his place."

Lili pulled one of the leases toward her and read with her chin in her hand. "This one says deposit. Five hundred damage deposit. That's normal, right? My cousin paid one."

"It says it right there." Jasmine tapped the line. "But it also says last month's rent deposit, and that's the full eleven hundred. So they want sixteen hundred up front, plus first month. That's more than I have."

She had been over this part twice already on the bus, and something about it kept snagging, the way a thread catches on a nail. Her mother had said, pay it, that's how it works, everyone pays it. Her mother had also said, when Jasmine pointed out that she would be seventeen and signing a legal document, don't get clever. Jasmine had not felt clever. She had felt like she was standing at the shallow end of something deep, and everyone ahead of her was already swimming.

Lionel came in with his headphones around his neck and a bag of clementines, which he distributed like a man who believed fruit could solve most problems. He read the deposit lines with his mouth slightly open. "Mine asked for last month's rent and that was it," he said. "I don't remember a damage deposit."

"Maybe it's a new thing," Lili said.

"Maybe it's a made-up thing," Jasmine said, and the moment she said it she heard how it sounded, how ready she was to denigrate a landlord she had never met, simply because the number was inconvenient. She flushed a little. "I mean. Maybe. I don't actually know."

Ms. Augustin, who worked at the desk near the alcove and had already helped Jasmine set up her first student account that morning, came over with a form in her hand and paused when she saw the papers. "Are those leases?"

"Sort of a crisis," Lili said.

"Mine had a damage deposit when I was your age," Ms. Augustin said. "I paid it and I never saw it again, and I thought that was just the way of things." She set the form down, not as advice, more like a memory being placed on the table. "My nephew argued his, a few years ago. In Ontario a landlord can only collect a rent deposit, and it can't be more than one month's rent. Or one rent period, if you pay more often. A damage deposit they can't charge at all."

Jasmine wrote it down before she had finished hearing it, the pen moving ahead of her understanding. "They can't charge a damage deposit," she repeated. "Not they shouldn't. They can't."

"That's what he told me," Ms. Augustin said, and went back to her desk.

The three of them sat with that for a second. Lili broke the clementine in her hand and the smell rose sharp and sweet. "So the basement room," she said, "nine hundred all in, that's just nine hundred."

"Plus internet, call it thirty." Jasmine did the arithmetic twice, because the first time she didn't trust it. "Nine thirty. The studio, eleven hundred plus hydro, say eighty in the worst months, and it's not all in the worst months, so maybe seventy-five averaged. Call it eleven seventy-five. So the difference is around two hundred and forty a month."

"Which is," Lionel said, "two thousand eight hundred and eighty a year."

"I can do subtraction," Jasmine said, but she was smiling, because he had done it on his phone before she could and there was something comforting in that, in the way a friend's surplus energy could be borrowed for an afternoon.

She looked at the two pages side by side, the basement with its small window drawn in the floor plan like an apology, the studio with a balcony the size of a doormat. She was trying to hold two ideas at once, and they would not sit still. There was the arithmetic, clean and settled, the basement winning by nearly three thousand dollars a year. And there was the other ledger, the one no calculator would total: the basement was below grade, a lower stratum of every building, and she had read enough forum threads at two in the morning to know that some of them stayed damp and some of them stayed dark, and that a year is a long time to live in a room you chose for its price alone. The studio, meanwhile, would eat the money she had been quietly saving toward a spring trip that Lili had planned with an almost epicurean attention to detail, the good bakery, the good seats, the one perfect dinner. Two hundred and forty a month was that trip, gone.

"Which one," Lili said, "if you had to decide today."

"I don't have to decide today." Jasmine squared the pages. "That's the thing. I have until Friday. But the deposit is wrong no matter which one I pick, so I'm going to write to the studio people first and ask them to take it off. Politely. Because if they say no, or if they get strange about it, that tells me something too, and then the basement room gets better and better, damp or not."

"You're going to trust a landlord who's already tried one thing," Lionel said.

"I'm going to find out what they do when someone notices," Jasmine said. "That's different from trusting them."

She folded both leases and put them in the folder with her passport and the bank slips, and Lili held the door. Outside, the afternoon had gone the color of weak tea, and the bus was already at the corner. Jasmine ran for it, folder pressed flat against her chest, and made it just as the doors sighed shut behind her.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, called chemiosmosis, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
story:
The science museum would close at five, and Paige had until then to understand something she had failed to understand for three weeks. Her exam was tomorrow morning. She sat on the bench in front of the giant model cell, the one with the mitochondrion you could walk into, and opened her notebook to a page of arrows that still meant nothing to her. Glucose went in, ATP came out, and between those two things her notes dissolved into a mess of names like NADH and electron transport chain, which she had copied but never once felt in her hands.

Ian dropped onto the bench beside her with two sodas from the vending machine and handed her one without asking. "Still the ATP thing?" he said. He was the one who had habituated to the museum's smell, that mixture of floor wax and recycled air, because he came here every Saturday to sketch the dinosaur hall. Paige had never habituated to anything academic in her life; she had to fight for every concept like territory.

"Everything makes sense until the last step," she said. "Glucose breaks down, fine. Pyruvate, fine. And then the notes just say the energy gets turned into ATP, as if that's an answer instead of a question. Turned how? By what machine?"

Iyad arrived late, out of breath from the bus, holding his phone with a timer already running: forty minutes before the biology review session his cousin had scheduled for him at six, which meant forty minutes before he had to leave. He leaned over her notes and squinted. "We did this last week," he said. "Sort of. My uncle kept explaining it at dinner and I kept not listening."

They walked into the mitochondrion together. Inside, the membrane curved over their heads in soft folds, and small panels lit up in sequence along the wall. Protons, the panels said, accumulating on one side. Paige read it twice. Something about the word accumulating bothered her in a way she couldn't name, the way a wrong note in a familiar song bothers you before you can find it.

"It's like the farm," Iyad said suddenly. He was pointing at the panel with the pile-up of protons on one side of the membrane. "My uncle's village. There's a dam, and the water builds up behind it, and the pressure of all that water wanting to get through is what turns the turbine. It's not the water itself, it's the wanting." He looked almost embarrassed. "He used to say that when I was small. That the dam is just stored waiting."

Paige stood very still. In her mind the diagram reorganized itself, the arrows collapsing and rebuilding into something she could finally see: the protons crowding against the membrane the way water crowds behind a wall, the flow through it driving something downstream. "So the cell charges up one side of a membrane and lets it pour through," she said slowly. "That's the machine. That's the turning."

"Peter Mitchell figured that out," said a voice behind them. Mr. Kapoor, who had been her biology teacher two years ago and now volunteered as a docent on weekends, stood with his hands in his pockets and his museum badge hanging crooked. He wore the kind of obsolescent tie that had small molecules printed on it, a gift, she suspected, from somebody who loved physiology as much as he did. "Proposed it in 1961, that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane. Nobody believed him for years. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1978 for it."

"What's it called?" Paige asked. "The process. There's a word, isn't there?"

"Chemiosmosis," Mr. Kapoor said, and tapped the panel. "It's on the plaque, bottom corner."

She found the word there, small and certain, and copied it into her notebook next to her redrawn diagram. Iyad checked his phone and said he had twenty minutes, and Ian asked whether dams ever broke, and Mr. Kapoor said that in cells, more or less, they didn't, which was the whole point of a membrane. Paige sat down on the floor inside the model mitochondrion, her back against the warm plastic of the inner wall, and worked through the sequence one more time from glucose onward, saying it aloud under her breath while Iyad listened and corrected her once, gently, at the pyruvate step.

She still couldn't explain why the electrons moved the way they moved, or what NADH was actually doing in the middle of it all, and she wrote those two questions in the margin, underlined, honest. The overhead lights flicked once, the museum's five o'clock warning. Iyad gathered his bag and said he'd be late; Ian stayed sketching the folded membrane into his pad. Paige closed her notebook and ran her hand once along the curve of the wall, all that quiet crowding on the other side of it, waiting to pour through.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In his 1975 book Discipline and Punish, Michel Foucault used Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation.
story:
The yellow triangle appeared in the corner of Jessica's screen at 9:14 on Tuesday morning, and she knew it meant someone was watching. The new software, FocusTrack, had been installed on every machine in the computer science room over the weekend, and Mr. Chen had explained it in one sentence: if the triangle was lit, a proctor could see your screen. Nobody had asked what else it could see.

"Mine went yellow twice during the quiz," Kingston said at lunch, dropping his tray beside hers. "Twice. I wasn't even cheating, I was reading the question again."

"Then why did it flag you?"

"Because I looked away? Because I typed slow? Nobody tells you the rules." He stabbed his fork into the pasta. "Carys says hers never goes yellow."

That was the part Jessica couldn't stop turning over. Carys sat in the front row and typed fast and never opened extra tabs, and her triangle stayed grey and polite. Kingston slouched, opened a dictionary tab once, and got flagged. She had watched it happen, had watched him freeze when the light came on, had watched Mr. Chen drift over without being asked, as if the software had called him. Which, she supposed, it had.

The problem was simple and it wasn't going away: the software had already changed how Kingston worked. He had started typing with his hands stiff, positioning his face toward the screen like a man posing for a passport photo. And the school had a policy, buried in the handbook, that students could appeal a monitoring tool if they brought an argument to the technology committee. Jessica wanted to bring that argument. She just didn't have one yet that was more than a feeling.

In the city library that Thursday she found a shelf of philosophy nobody visited, and pulled down a fat book with a cracked spine. She had been hunting for something about surveillance, anything, and had written down a phrase the software's own website used, about visibility and compliance. The book was Discipline and Punish, by Michel Foucault, published in 1975, and in the middle of it he took up an old prison design by a man named Bentham called the panopticon. She read the passage twice on the carpet between the shelves. Foucault used the panopticon as a metaphor, she read, for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation. Not the fact of it. The possibility. You couldn't know whether the guard was in the tower, so you behaved as if he always was. The tower did the work even when empty.

Friday's class was a free work period, which meant the triangles did their quiet work while everyone coded. Mr. Chen moved between rows, glancing at screens the way he always had, and Jessica realized she could no longer tell the difference between his glance and the software's. That was the thing she had been trying to articulate all week. She raised her hand.

"Mr. Chen, is FocusTrack more like your glance or like a watchtower?"

He stopped. "A watchtower?"

"A panopticon," she said. "It's Bentham's prison design. Foucault used it in Discipline and Punish, in 1975, as a metaphor for how institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation. You look at our screens and we can see you looking. The software watches and we can't tell when. That's the difference."

From two rows back, Kingston's triangle glowed yellow at the sound of his name being nowhere in the sentence at all, only at his sudden turn toward the front.

The committee met the following Wednesday in the conference room with the good chairs. Mr. Chen had signed her form without comment, which she took as either support or neutrality, and Carys came to speak for the software, which Jessica had not expected. "It caught two kids copying last semester," Carys said, arms folded, "before this it was just a rumor and nobody was ever sure. My scores mean something now." And that was the truth too, Jessica thought; Carys's rectitude was real, her desire to have honest work recognized was not fake, and the software had genuinely served it. But the same software had taught a boy who read slowly to be afraid of looking away from his screen, and nobody had chosen that, and nobody could opt out of it.

"I'm not saying take it down tomorrow," Jessica said, when the chair of the committee, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, gestured to her. "I'm saying we should know what it is. It's not a teacher's glance. A glance is human, it's accountable, you can meet the eyes. This is the possibility of being watched all the time, with no way to check. That changes how we work before it ever catches anything."

She had cogitated on it for three nights, both sides of it, and had decided she could only be honest about what stayed uncertain: the flags might be catching real cheating sometimes, or they might just be punishing the way certain people moved. She had tested it herself, opening the same dictionary tab on two machines, one from her seat and one borrowed during lunch, and only one had gone yellow, and she could not explain why. She told the committee that too, the unexplained result, the small epicurean pleasure she'd felt watching the machine fail to be consistent, and immediately felt ashamed of the pleasure.

The committee did not vote that day. They said they would review the vendor's flagging criteria, whatever those were, and consider a transparency notice on every screen. Mr. Chen walked her out.

"You know I argued for the software," he said in the hallway. "Two years ago. I thought it would save me time."

"Does it?"

He looked at the classroom door, then at her. "It saves time," he said. "That's all I can say for it."

Behind them, through the door's narrow window, the row of monitors glowed with their grey triangles, patient as towers, and Jessica watched until the light on Kingston's machine flickered yellow, once, for no reason anyone in the room could name.

The restaurant had pushed its tables together wrong, so Maya ended up wedged between her grandfather and Annika, half facing the big screen bolted above the bar, where the final game of the playoffs glowed in patient blue and white. Her grandfather had claimed this corner booth an hour before puck drop, the way other men his age reserved opera seats. He'd ordered a second iced tea before the first was gone and kept looking at the screen like it might blink out.

"Who's winning?" Annika asked, though the score was on the screen in digits tall enough to read from the parking lot.

"The team that scores more goals," Maya's grandfather said, and Maya laughed before she could stop herself, because he was completely sincere.

Maya had come for the wings and for Annika, not for hockey. She'd spent the year telling anyone who asked that sports were just tribal arithmetic, people emotionally investing in random geography. But watching her grandfather watch the game kept snagging her attention. When a player held the puck too long, his whole face tightened; when a shot rang off the post, he made a small sound like a word he'd swallowed. It was ridiculous. It was also, she had to admit, something she understood nothing about, and that bothered her more than she'd expected. What was in it? What were they all actually looking at?

"They're playing for the Cup," her grandfather said during a commercial, as if he'd heard her wondering. Ronan, across the table, leaned in. "The Stanley Cup. Lord Stanley of Preston donated it in 1892. First awarded in 1893. Oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America." He said it flat, the way he recited things, then went back to his mozzarella sticks.

"Existing," Maya repeated. She liked that word in the sentence, the way it hinted at trophies that hadn't survived, whole competitions gone to ash or landfills while this one silver bowl kept circulating from hand to hand for longer than anyone in this restaurant had been alive. "So it's older than every player, every coach, every franchise?"

"Older than the restaurant," Ronan said. "Older than the restaurant's grandparents."

Annika, who wanted to be a sports agent and had been describing contract law all evening, said players' agents had fiduciary duties, they had to put the player's interest first, and that she found the whole system both elegant and grim. Then someone on the screen took a cheap hit and the bar crowd turned vitriolic, shouting things at the referee that Annika's future profession would definitely not endorse, and Maya's grandfather stood halfway up before sitting back down, jaw working.

Maya had planned to spend the period after dinner equivocating about it all, telling Annika sports were fine for other people, she could take it or leave it. Instead she found herself asking her grandfather why he cared, and he didn't exactly answer. He said his father had watched the Canadiens on a radio that only worked when you slapped it. He said the Cup had been dropped in a swimming pool once, or maybe that was another trophy, he couldn't remember, and he waved his hand as if the uncertainty didn't matter, or as if it did, and that was the point. A thing that old belongs to everyone who ever held it and no one, Maya thought. It gets passed along like a story that changes a little every time and somehow stays the same. She didn't say this out loud. She was still testing whether she believed it.

In the third period the game tied, then untied, then tied again, and Maya realized she was leaning forward with everyone else, her hand around a cold glass she'd forgotten drinking from. When her team scored, she was on her feet, and Annika was screaming, and Ronan had both hands in the air, and her grandfather was laughing at her, actually laughing, and she laughed back at him because there was nothing to defend. She had changed her mind in public and didn't feel like explaining it.

The horn sounded. On the screen, grown men fell into each other and wept, and somewhere a trophy older than the building they stood in was about to be carried out onto the ice. Her grandfather paid the check, counting out bills with slow ceremony. He looked at Maya across the table, at her flushed face, and raised one eyebrow.

"Same booth next June?" he said.
